ABSTRACT

Modern enterprise and industrial cyber-physical networks face increasingly sophisticated, low-latency cyber threats, ranging from volumetric denial-of-service and lateral reconnaissance to supply-chain tampering and prompt-injection vectors targeting cognitive security systems. To counter these attacks, modern security operations centers increasingly explore hybrid Real-Time Network Intrusion Detection Systems (RT-IDS) coupled with autonomous Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) containment mechanisms. This thesis presents a comprehensive, master's-thesis-grade technical audit, empirical benchmark, and critical evaluation of CyberGuard, an open-source hybrid intrusion detection and guarded containment framework.

Adhering strictly to empirical evidence rules, this investigation combines static byte-and-AST source code auditing (disaggregating the 113,107 total repository lines into 31,865 Python source lines [27,750 SLOC across 139 files], 9,682 Python test lines [7,756 SLOC across 44 files], 6,917 frontend JS/HTML/CSS lines [6,223 SLOC across 13 files], 12,606 documentation and configuration lines [11,816 SLOC across 31 files], 617 automation and operational script lines [513 SLOC across 8 files], and 51,420 dataset, raw fixture, and binary asset lines [49,053 SLOC across 64 files] across exactly 299 total files), dependency forensics, and an exhaustive experimental test battery. Crucially, the repository encompasses two distinct model architectures: (1) a bundled synthetic-trained model (data/models/trained/) serving as an evaluation fixture across 4 classes, and (2) a newly integrated candidate pipeline (data/models/candidate_cicids2017/) trained on 2.097 million real CICIDS2017 network flows across 8 classes, retained strictly in shadow evaluation mode (shadow_only_not_promoted, production_approved=false).

We test seven critical hypotheses (H1H_1H1​ through H7H_7H7​). First, we confirm (H1H_1H1​) that the bundled detection model was trained on an artificial synthetic fixture (sample_traffic.csv, seed 42) with hand-set Gaussian/exponential distributions across only four classes (Benign, Bot, DDoS, PortScan), rendering claimed laboratory accuracies (96.25%) scientifically unrepresentative of real traffic. When evaluated on real CICIDS2017 traffic, the bundled model suffers catastrophic collapse down to 38.15% accuracy and 0.0757 Macro-F1, triggering false alarms on 55.07% of benign flows. Second, while the real-data candidate model achieves a high headline accuracy (98.49%) and Weighted-F1 (0.9855 [95% CI: 0.9852, 0.9860]), this metric is heavily dominated by Benign traffic (84.8% of the test partition). Macro-F1 (0.6852 [95% CI: 0.6447, 0.7133]) unmasks severe operational blind spots: complete detection collapse on Bot traffic (0.00% recall, 0.00 F1 across 113 samples), poor precision on PortScan (0.1862), and severe variance on Infiltration (support = 7, rendering its 0.80 F1 statistically uninterpretable). Third, we expose critical methodological decisions in the candidate workflow: silent resolution of 6,132 exact and 3,228 near conflicting duplicate rows by first-seen CSV order; an optimistic row-order capture_group split that conceals temporal drift; and an autoencoder trained only on the first 100,000 benign rows that exhibits higher reconstruction error on benign test traffic than on attack traffic. Fourth, we expose severe train/serve feature skew: forcing features to live sniffer values collapses candidate Macro-F1 to 0.3668, while Suricata approximations drop it to 0.2840. Fifth, under a strict day-disjoint split (Mon–Wed train vs. Thu–Fri test), unseen attack miss rates jump to 65.69% ± 16.65%. Finally, we formulate a mechatronic cyber-physical safety interlock framework reconciling network containment with ISO 13849 robotic safety requirements.

Keywords: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS), Machine Learning in Cybersecurity, Train/Serve Skew, Empirical Software Forensics, Autonomous Containment, Formal Verification, SMT Solvers, Mechatronics Security, IEC 62443, Cyber-Physical Systems.

ملخص الأطروحة (ARABIC ABSTRACT)

تواجه الشبكات المؤسسية والأنظمة السيبرانية-الفيزيائية المعاصرة تهديدات أمنية متقدمة وفائقة السرعة، تتراوح بين هجمات الحرمان من الخدمة الحجمية (DDoS) والاستطلاع الشبكي الخفي، وصولاً إلى استهداف أدوات الذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي عبر هجمات حقن الأوامر (Prompt Injection). ولمواجهة هذه المخاطر، اتجهت مراكز العمليات الأمنية نحو تبني أنظمة كشف التسلل الشبكي الهجينة في الوقت الحقيقي (RT-IDS) المدمجة بمحركات الاحتواء الدفاعي الذاتي والتحكم الآلي (SOAR). تقدم هذه الأطروحة دراسة أكاديمية نقدية وتدقيقاً جنائياً برمجياً شاملاً، مدعوماً بتقييم تجريبي معملي، لمنظومة CyberGuard مفتوحة المصدر للكشف عن التسلل والتحييد التلقائي للتهديدات.

انطلاقاً من قواعد الحقيقة الصارمة القائمة على الأدلة المباشرة، يجمع هذا البحث بين التدقيق البرمجي الثابت للشفرة المصدرية (مع تفصيل إجمالي أسطر المستودع البالغة 113,107 أسطر إلى: 31,865 سطراً لمصدر بايثون [27,750 سطر برمجي عبر 139 ملفاً]، و 9,682 سطراً لاختبارات بايثون [7,756 سطر برمجي عبر 44 ملفاً]، و 6,917 سطراً لواجهات الويب JS/HTML/CSS [6,223 سطر برمجي عبر 13 ملفاً]، و 12,606 أسطر لملفات التوثيق والإعدادات [11,816 سطر برمجي عبر 31 ملفاً]، و 617 سطراً لنصوص الأتمتة والتشغيل [513 سطر برمجي عبر 8 ملفات]، و 51,420 سطراً لملفات البيانات والعينات والأصول الثنائية [49,053 سطر برمجي عبر 64 ملفاً] ضمن 299 ملفاً إجمالياً للمستودع)، وفحص نماذج التعلم الآلي المحفوظة، وتشغيل بطارية اختبارات إجهاد وتجارب استنساخية كاملة. وتفحص الأطروحة بنية النموذجين في المستودع: (1) النموذج المدمج المدرب على بيانات اصطناعية كعينة فحص، و (2) نموذج المرشح المستقل المدرب على بيانات حقيقية من مجموعة CICIDS2017 عبر 2.097 مليون تدفق شبكي، والمحفوظ حصرياً في وضع التقييم الخفي دون ترقية تشغيلية (shadow_only_not_promoted).

اختبرت الأطروحة سبع فرضيات علمية أساسية (H1H_1H1​ إلى H7H_7H7​)؛ حيث تم إثبات أن النموذج المدمج (H1H_1H1​) يعاني من انهيار كارثي عند اختباره على بيانات شبكية حقيقية، حيث تهبط دقته من 96.25% إلى 38.15% ومعدل Macro-F1 إلى 0.0757، مع إطلاق إنذارات زائفة على 55.07% من تدفقات البيانات البريئة. ورغم تحقيق نموذج المرشح المدرب على البيانات الحقيقية دقة ظاهرية بلغت 98.49% ومعدل Weighted-F1 قدره 0.9855، إلا أن هذا المقياس مضلل بسبب هيمنة التدفقات البريئة (84.8% من البيانات)، بينما كشف معدل Macro-F1 البالغ 0.6852 عن فشل كلي في كشف هجمات البوتنت (Bot) بمعدل استدعاء 0.00% ودقة ضعيفة في كشف هجمات مسح المنافذ PortScan (0.1862). كما كشف التدقيق عن قرارات منهجية حساسة: حل التعارض في 6,132 صفاً متطابقاً بحسب أسبقية الظهور، وتقسيم البيانات بناءً على ترتيب الصفوف مما يمنح نتائج مفرطة التفاؤل، وانحراف التدريب والتشغيل الذي يخفض مقياس Macro-F1 إلى 0.3668 عند تطبيق قيود ملتقط الحزم المباشر، وتخطي نسبة إفلات الهجمات غير المرئية حاجز 65.69% عند اختبار نموذج مقسم على أساس الأيام المستقلة. واختتمت الأطروحة بطرح منظور هندسة الميكاترونكس لحماية الشبكات الصناعية الروبوتية وفق معايير الأمان الوظيفي (IEC 62443 و ISO 13849).

الكلمات المفتاحية: كشف التسلل الشبكي (NIDS)، التعلم الآلي في الأمن السيبراني، انحراف التدريب والتشغيل، التدقيق الجنائي للبرمجيات، الاحتواء التلقائي، التحقق الصوري، محللات SMT، أمن الميكاترونكس، معيار IEC 62443، الأنظمة السيبرانية-الفيزيائية.

CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION

1.1 Motivation and Context

In contemporary cybersecurity operations, modern enterprise networks and cyber-physical infrastructures face an unprecedented surge in both the velocity and sophistication of cyber attacks. The threat landscape has transitioned from manual, single-stage penetrations to automated, distributed attack vectors. Adversaries routinely deploy automated botnets, high-volume Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) campaigns, evasive port scanning, lateral credential dumping, and advanced ransomware [1]. Furthermore, the rapid enterprise integration of cognitive artificial intelligence—specifically Large Language Models (LLMs) used for security incident analysis, autonomous triage, and report generation—has introduced novel attack surfaces, most notably adversarial prompt injection and data poisoning [2], [3].

To defend against these multi-faceted threats, Security Operations Centers (SOCs) have increasingly moved beyond traditional, purely signature-based Intrusion Detection Systems (such as Snort or Suricata [4], [5]). While signature engines excel at identifying known Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) with near-zero false positive rates, they are fundamentally blind to zero-day vulnerabilities, novel polymorphic payloads, and stealthy behavioral anomalies. Consequently, the academic and industrial security communities have heavily invested in Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) approaches for Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) [6], [7]. These systems typically analyze summarized network telemetry—represented as bidirectional communication flows (5-tuples: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol)—and classify traffic based on statistical, temporal, and volumetric properties extracted from packet sequences [1], [8].

Fig. 1. Conceptual Overview of Modern Hybrid RT-IDS in Contemporary SOC Operations.

However, detection alone is insufficient in modern operational environments. When high-bandwidth attacks strike, human security analysts experience severe alert fatigue; mean time to detect (MTTD) and mean time to respond (MTTR) often range from tens of minutes to several days [9], [10]. This operational gap has catalyzed the emergence of Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms and autonomous cyber-defense engines capable of executing containment actions—such as dynamic firewall rule insertion, active network socket severance, or malicious process termination—at machine speed [10], [11].

1.2 Problem Statement

Despite extensive research into ML-based intrusion detection, translating laboratory models into production-grade systems remains fraught with fundamental engineering, statistical, and safety challenges. As established in the seminal works of Sommer and Paxson [6] and Arp et al. [12], machine learning applied to computer security operates in an environment characterized by:

  1. Extreme Class Imbalance and the Base-Rate Fallacy: In real-world enterprise traffic, malicious flows constitute a microscopic fraction (often <0.001%< 0.001\%<0.001%) of total network activity. Under Axelsson's base-rate fallacy [13], even an intrusion detection model boasting an apparently stellar 99.9%99.9\%99.9% accuracy and a 1%1\%1% False Positive Rate (FPR) will generate thousands of false alarms per day, completely drowning out legitimate security alerts.
  2. Train/Serve Skew and Flawed Benchmarks: Many academic models are trained and evaluated on public benchmark datasets (such as KDD Cup 99, NSL-KDD, and CICIDS2017 [1], [14]). However, rigorous independent audits—such as that by Engelen et al. [15]—have uncovered critical bugs in feature extraction utilities (e.g., CICFlowMeter), erroneous ground-truth labeling, and artificial network simulation artifacts that inflate reported evaluation metrics. When an IDS relies on synthetic fixtures generated via simple random distributions rather than real packet captures, the resulting models exhibit zero real-world operational efficacy.
  3. The Self-Inflicted Denial of Service (Self-DoS) Dilemma: Granting automated software the authority to execute containment actions introduces acute existential risk. An adversarial attacker can forge spoofed network packets or manipulate automated response logic to trigger countermeasures against critical infrastructure assets—such as domain controllers, core DNS resolvers, default gateways, or critical process threads—effectively turning the defensive system into a weapon of self-destruction [9], [16].
  4. Cognitive Latency and Fragility in Generative AI: Incorporating advisory Large Language Models (LLMs) into real-time decision loops creates massive latency bottlenecks. Local edge inference on constrained hardware frequently introduces multi-second delays, while LLMs remain prone to syntactic formatting errors and adversarial prompt injections [2], [17].

The software repository audited in this thesis—CyberGuard (RT-IDS)—represents a contemporary architectural attempt to solve these challenges through a hybrid architecture combining line-rate packet capture, a 4-stage classifier-first pipeline, mathematical formal safety invariants, and an advisory cognitive layer. However, previous preliminary audits suggested potential discrepancies between documented claims and actual source code behavior. A rigorous, independent academic investigation is required to establish the true capabilities, limitations, and empirical realities of the system.

1.3 Research Questions

This thesis investigates the following primary research questions:

  • RQ1RQ_1RQ1​ (Line-Rate Flow Assembly & Edge Telemetry): Can a pure-Python raw socket packet capture and flow aggregation engine accurately assemble bidirectional transport-layer flows at multi-thousand packet-per-second rates, handle asynchronous TCP stateful teardowns without creating ghost flows, and extract valid network statistics across both Windows and Linux hosts?
  • RQ2RQ_2RQ2​ (Train/Serve Skew & Feature Parity): To what extent do synthetic approximations and static constants within streaming log adapters (such as Suricata EVE tailers) deviate from the theoretical definitions of standard flow features, and what impact does this skew have on downstream anomaly detectors?
  • RQ3RQ_3RQ3​ (Mathematical Reality of Formal Safety Guarantees): How are theoretical First-Order Logic safety invariants and "SMT formal verification" implemented in practice within autonomous mitigation engines, and do production tools genuinely execute automated theorem proving (e.g., via Z3 or CVC5) or rely on symbolic propositional approximations?
  • RQ4RQ_4RQ4​ (Cognitive Architecture & Adversarial Robustness): What are the measured latency, throughput, and false-positive characteristics of integrating retrieval-augmented generative AI into automated security triage pipelines, and how does heuristic severity coupling affect benign enterprise operations?
  • RQ5RQ_5RQ5​ (Cyber-Physical and Mechatronics Adaptability): How can an automated intrusion detection and containment architecture be modified to protect real-time industrial robotics and mechatronic automation cells (operating over Modbus TCP, EtherNet/IP, and OPC UA) without violating physical safety interlocks (ISO 13849/IEC 62443)?

1.4 Aim and Objectives

The primary aim of this research is to perform an exhaustive, evidence-based academic audit, empirical performance evaluation, and architectural analysis of the CyberGuard RT-IDS codebase, culminating in a verifiable blueprint for mechatronic industrial network defense.

To achieve this aim, the investigation executes the following specific objectives:

  1. Module-by-Module Source Code Forensics: Perform deep static code analysis and AST decomposition across the entire codebase (backend/, cyberguard/, scripts/, frontend/), documenting verifiable line-number evidence for every claim and inspecting component trust boundaries.
  2. Empirical Verification of Pre-Audit Hypotheses (H1H_1H1​ to H7H_7H7​): Systematically evaluate seven audit hypotheses regarding model training lineage, socket sniffing limitations, feature approximations, documentation contradictions, formal verification claims, test counts, and pickle deserialization risks.
  3. Reproducible Experimental Benchmarking: Build and execute automated experimental test harnesses to measure raw packet processing throughput, pipeline inference latency distributions (P50P_{50}P50​, P90P_{90}P90​, P95P_{95}P95​, P99P_{99}P99​), batch throughput scaling, memory footprint, and confusion matrices on local hardware.
  4. Threat Modeling and Security Assessment: Conduct an exhaustive STRIDE security audit, analyzing deserialization risks, role-based access control, two-person rule enforcement, and rollback receipt integrity.
  5. Formulation of an Industrial Mechatronics Defense Model: Synthesize the findings into a proposed, domain-specific architecture adapted for industrial control systems (ICS) and robotic manufacturing cells, reconciling autonomous network isolation with human functional safety standards.

1.5 Scope and Operational Boundaries

This investigation operates under strict methodological and operational boundaries:

  • Evidence-Only Rule: In accordance with rigorous scientific standards, no performance metrics, accuracy figures, latency percentiles, or code assertions are stated without verifiable traces to raw experimental run outputs (logged under report/results/) or direct source code lines ([CE-xx]).
  • Non-Destructive Local Testing: All dynamic capture, live sniffing, and actuator execution experiments were conducted in isolated, non-production test environments on a dedicated Windows 11 host. Host containment actuators were audited primarily in simulation mode to prevent disruption to operating system services.
  • Academic Citation Integrity: All cited peer-reviewed literature, official RFC specifications, and industrial standards were individually verified via authoritative academic repositories (IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, USENIX, arXiv) with direct DOI or official URL links. Unverifiable sources were excluded.
  • Distinction Between Implemented Code and Future Proposals: Clear demarcation is maintained throughout this document between audited source code as currently committed in the repository, and proposed architectural extensions (such as the Mechatronics framework in Chapter 9).

CHAPTER 2: BACKGROUND AND LITERATURE REVIEW

2.1 Evolution of Network Intrusion Detection Systems

Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) constitute a foundational pillar in enterprise network defense, designed to continuously inspect passing communications and identify unauthorized access, policy violations, or malicious exploitation. Over the past three decades, intrusion detection technologies have undergone significant architectural evolution, transitioning from rudimentary stateless packet filtering to stateful protocol analysis, distributed flow-based statistical modeling, and contemporary neuro-symbolic hybrid frameworks [6], [18].

timeline title Evolution of Network Intrusion Detection Paradigms 1990s : Stateless Packet Filters (BPF) : Signature Pattern Matching (Snort) : Stateful Protocol Reassembly (Bro/Zeek) 2000s : DARPA & KDD'99 Benchmarks : Statistical Anomaly Detection : Base-Rate Fallacy Formalized 2010s : High-Rate Flow Metering (CICFlowMeter) : Supervised Tree Ensembles (XGBoost, RF) : Autoencoder Anomaly Scoring (Kitsune) 2020s : MITRE ATT&CK & D3FEND Ontologies : SMT Formal Safety Invariants : Cognitive Advisory LLMs & SOAR
Fig. 2. Evolution of Network Intrusion Detection Systems from Packet Filtering to Neuro-Symbolic Ensembles.

Early intrusion detection systems operated primarily at the network and transport layers using primitive pattern-matching rules. In 1993, McCanne and Jacobson introduced the Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) [19], establishing an in-kernel, register-based virtual machine capable of filtering raw packet streams at high link speeds without incurring excessive user-space context-switching overhead. Building upon packet filtering, Roesch released Snort in 1999 [4], which codified rule-based signature matching by scanning raw payload bytes for regular expressions and static byte signatures. Concurrently, Paxson introduced the Bro network monitor (now Zeek) [8], pioneering stateful connection tracking and application-layer protocol reassembly. While signature engines remain indispensable due to their deterministic predictability and high processing throughput, their reliance on static indicators of compromise renders them ineffective against novel zero-day exploits, dynamic evasion techniques, and encrypted payloads.

2.2 Flow-Based Network Telemetry and Feature Engineering

As network line speeds scaled from megabits to gigabits and tens of gigabits per second, deep packet inspection (DPI) of every packet payload became computationally prohibitive on commodity hardware. Furthermore, the ubiquitous adoption of Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.2 / TLS 1.3) rendered packet payloads opaque. In response, modern NIDS shifted toward flow-based network telemetry.

A network flow is formally defined as a unidirectional or bidirectional sequence of packets sharing a common 5-tuple identifier within a bounded time window [1]:

Flow Key=⟨IPsrc,IPdst,Portsrc,Portdst,Protocol⟩\text{Flow Key} = \langle \text{IP}_{\text{src}}, \text{IP}_{\text{dst}}, \text{Port}_{\text{src}}, \text{Port}_{\text{dst}}, \text{Protocol} \rangleFlow Key=⟨IPsrc​,IPdst​,Portsrc​,Portdst​,Protocol⟩

Bidirectional flow assembly aggregates both forward traffic (client to server) and backward traffic (server to client). Flows are statefully tracked and demarcated using two distinct temporal mechanisms:

  1. Active Timeout (τactive\tau_{\text{active}}τactive​): The maximum allowable duration for an active flow (typically 120 seconds). When a persistent connection exceeds this bound, the accumulated metrics are flushed to downstream inference engines, and a new sub-flow record is instantiated.
  2. Idle Timeout (τidle\tau_{\text{idle}}τidle​): The maximum permissible silence interval between successive packets (typically 15 to 30 seconds). If no packet matching the 5-tuple is observed within τidle\tau_{\text{idle}}τidle​, the flow is marked complete.
  3. TCP Connection Teardown Flags: For Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) traffic [20], observation of a Reset (RST) flag indicates abrupt termination, triggering immediate flow closure. Similarly, bidirectional FIN handshakes signal orderly connection termination.

Feature extraction utilities—most prominently the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity's CICFlowMeter [1]—compute statistical summaries over the flow lifetime. These include volumetric packet and byte counts, inter-arrival time (IAT) statistics, packet length distributions (mean, standard deviation, extrema), transport-layer flag counts (SYN, ACK, FIN, RST, PSH, URG), and initial TCP window advertisements (Init_Win_bytes_fwd, Init_Win_bytes_bwd). These features form the standard tabular input vectors consumed by machine learning classifiers.

2.3 The Benchmark Dilemma in Network Intrusion Detection

The development and empirical validation of machine learning algorithms for network intrusion detection depends fundamentally on the quality, realism, and labeling accuracy of benchmark datasets. Over the past two decades, several major benchmarks have driven the academic literature, as summarized in Table I.

TABLE I. Comparison of Major Intrusion Detection Benchmarks and Documented Limitations.
Dataset Year Source / Publisher Capture Type Documented Vulnerabilities & Scientific Limitations Key Citation
DARPA 98/99 1999 MIT Lincoln Laboratory Emulated network testbed Synthetic background traffic generated via Poisson distributions; lack of realistic user behavioral variation; outdated attack profiles. [14]
KDD Cup 99 1999 ACM SIGKDD / UCI Derived from DARPA 98 Catastrophic sample duplication (78% training and 75% testing duplicate rows); biased classifier performance toward frequent attacks; unrealistic class balance. [14]
NSL-KDD 2009 University of New Brunswick Filtered KDD Cup 99 Removed duplicate records and tuned difficulty levels, but retained artificial 1998 network topologies and obsolete operating system vulnerabilities. [14]
ISCX 2012 2012 Univ. of New Brunswick (ISCX) Systematic user profiles Introduced dynamic alpha/beta profile generator, but lacked modern encrypted traffic and multi-vector attack scenarios. [21]
CICIDS2017 2018 Canadian Inst. for Cybersecurity B-Profile testbed Widely adopted, but plagued by severe extraction tool artifacts, misordered packets, faulty label generation, and packet loss. [1], [15]
CSE-CIC-IDS2018 2018 AWS / CIC Cloud infrastructure Large-scale capture (16M flows), but shares identical CICFlowMeter extraction bugs and feature anomalies with CICIDS2017. [15], [18]

In 2009, Tavallaee et al. published their landmark analysis of KDD Cup 99 [14], revealing that over 78%78\%78% of training samples and 75%75\%75% of testing samples were exact duplicates. This rampant duplication artificially inflated the reported accuracy of superficial classifiers, leading to the creation of the NSL-KDD dataset. However, both datasets represented synthetic network architectures from the late 1990s, completely missing modern protocols, mobile traffic, and distributed attack structures.

To address these shortcomings, Sharafaldin, Lashkari, and Ghorbani introduced CICIDS2017 in 2018 [1]. Captured over a 5-day period in a multi-server testbed, it incorporated contemporary attack vectors, including Brute Force, Heartbleed, Botnet activity, DoS/DDoS, Web Attacks, and Infiltration, extracted into 80 features via CICFlowMeter. It rapidly became the dominant de facto benchmark in machine learning security research.

2.4 Documented Flaws in the CICIDS2017 Benchmark

Despite its widespread adoption across thousands of peer-reviewed publications, subsequent independent forensic evaluations revealed that CICIDS2017 suffers from severe methodological and technical flaws. In a seminal 2021 investigation published at the IEEE Security and Privacy Workshops (SPW), Engelen, Rimmer, and Joosen conducted a deep forensic reconstruction of the CICIDS2017 generation pipeline [15].

Engelen et al. identified three critical failure modes:

  1. Extraction Tool Artifacts (CICFlowMeter Bugs): The underlying Java-based CICFlowMeter utility suffered from fatal multi-threading race conditions, TCP out-of-order packet misassembly, and internal clock desynchronization. In multi-packet flows, forward and backward packet directions were frequently inverted, leading to negative inter-arrival times (IAT<0IAT < 0IAT<0) and incorrect initial window advertisements.
  2. Ground-Truth Labeling Inaccuracies: Automated labeling scripts assigned ground-truth labels strictly based on predefined IP address and timestamp ranges. When background benign user agents communicated with compromised servers during an attack window, legitimate HTTP requests were erroneously labeled as malicious attacks. Conversely, incomplete attack executions were labeled as benign. Engelen et al. proved that over 25%25\%25% of the total traffic volume contained erroneous or corrupted flow records [15].
  3. Synthetic Determinism and Tautological Learning: Because background traffic was generated using semi-deterministic automated execution scripts (B-Profiles), machine learning models frequently latched onto superficial artifacts—such as constant packet lengths or deterministic time deltas—rather than genuine attack dynamics. Models exhibiting 99.9%99.9\%99.9% laboratory accuracy on CICIDS2017 collapsed completely when deployed onto live enterprise networks.

2.5 Machine Learning Pitfalls in Computer Security

The failure of benchmark-trained models to generalize in operational environments has been comprehensively analyzed in the methodological literature. In their award-winning USENIX Security 2022 treatise, "Dos and Don'ts of Machine Learning in Computer Security," Arp et al. categorized ten pervasive pitfalls across the machine learning security lifecycle [12], as visualized in Fig. 3.

Feature Processing"] P3["P3: Data Snooping / Leakage"] P4["P4: Spurious Correlations"] P5["P5: Concept Drift & Temporal Bias"] end subgraph Sub_Sys ["3. System Design"] P6["P6: Inappropriate Baselines"] P7["P7: Inappropriate Metrics"] end subgraph Sub_Eval ["4. Evaluation"] P8["P8: Base Rate Fallacy"] P9["P9: Lab-Only Evaluation"] P10["P10: Compartmentalized Threat Models"] end P1 --> P3 P2 --> P4 P3 --> P6 P4 --> P7 P5 --> P8 P6 --> P9 P7 --> P10
Fig. 3. Methodological Pitfalls Across the Machine Learning Security Pipeline, based on Arp et al. [12].

Among these pitfalls, several are directly relevant to network intrusion detection:

  • Pitfall P3 (Data Snooping and Spatial Leakage): Occurs when information from the test dataset inadvertently leaks into the training pipeline. A common manifestation is performing global feature normalization (e.g., standard scaling or min-max normalization) over the entire dataset prior to splitting into train and test partitions.
  • Pitfall P5 (Concept Drift and Temporal Bias): Network protocols and threat behaviors evolve continuously. As demonstrated by Pendlebury et al. in their TESSERACT framework [22], random row splitting (e.g., standard 80/20 train/test splits via train_test_split) destroys temporal ordering, training on future packets to predict past packets and yielding wildly over-optimistic performance metrics. Legitimate validation demands strictly temporal, time-bounded splits.
  • Pitfall P8 (The Base Rate Fallacy): First formalized in intrusion detection by Axelsson in 2000 [13], Bayes' theorem demonstrates that the posterior probability of an intrusion given an alarm, P(I∣A)P(I|A)P(I∣A), is governed by the attack base rate P(I)P(I)P(I):
P(I∣A)=P(A∣I)P(I)P(A∣I)P(I)+P(A∣¬I)P(¬I)P(I|A) = \frac{P(A|I) P(I)}{P(A|I) P(I) + P(A|\neg I) P(\neg I)}P(I∣A)=P(A∣I)P(I)+P(A∣¬I)P(¬I)P(A∣I)P(I)​

If P(I)=10−5P(I) = 10^{-5}P(I)=10−5 (one attack flow per 100,000 flows), even an exceptional true positive rate P(A∣I)=0.999P(A|I) = 0.999P(A∣I)=0.999 and a low false positive rate P(A∣¬I)=0.001P(A|\neg I) = 0.001P(A∣¬I)=0.001 yields:

P(I∣A)=0.999×10−5(0.999×10−5)+(0.001×0.99999)≈0.000009990.00000999+0.00099999≈0.00989≈0.99%P(I|A) = \frac{0.999 \times 10^{-5}}{(0.999 \times 10^{-5}) + (0.001 \times 0.99999)} \approx \frac{0.00000999}{0.00000999 + 0.00099999} \approx 0.00989 \approx 0.99\%P(I∣A)=(0.999×10−5)+(0.001×0.99999)0.999×10−5​≈0.00000999+0.000999990.00000999​≈0.00989≈0.99%

Thus, over 99%99\%99% of triggered alarms are false positives!

2.6 Ensembles and Anomaly Detection Algorithms

To mitigate these limitations, state-of-the-art intrusion detection architectures rely on a combination of supervised classification algorithms and unsupervised anomaly detectors.

2.6.1 Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (XGBoost)

Introduced by Chen and Guestrin in 2016 [23], XGBoost is an optimized distributed gradient boosting library implementing tree ensembles:

y^i=∑k=1Kfk(xi),fk∈F\hat{y}_i = \sum_{k=1}^K f_k(x_i), \quad f_k \in \mathcal{F}y^​i​=k=1∑K​fk​(xi​),fk​∈F

where each fkf_kfk​ is an independent Classification and Regression Tree (CART). XGBoost optimizes a second-order Taylor expansion of the objective function incorporating regularized model complexity:

L(t)≈∑i=1n[l(yi,y^i(t−1))+gift(xi)+12hift2(xi)]+Ω(ft)\mathcal{L}^{(t)} \approx \sum_{i=1}^n \left[ l(y_i, \hat{y}_i^{(t-1)}) + g_i f_t(x_i) + \frac{1}{2} h_i f_t^2(x_i) \right] + \Omega(f_t)L(t)≈i=1∑n​[l(yi​,y^​i(t−1)​)+gi​ft​(xi​)+21​hi​ft2​(xi​)]+Ω(ft​)

where gi=∂y^(t−1)l(yi,y^(t−1))g_i = \partial_{\hat{y}^{(t-1)}} l(y_i, \hat{y}^{(t-1)})gi​=∂y^​(t−1)​l(yi​,y^​(t−1)) and hi=∂y^(t−1)2l(yi,y^(t−1))h_i = \partial^2_{\hat{y}^{(t-1)}} l(y_i, \hat{y}^{(t-1)})hi​=∂y^​(t−1)2​l(yi​,y^​(t−1)) are the first and second-order gradients. XGBoost offers exceptional predictive power on tabular flow features, fast inference execution, and built-in handling of missing values.

2.6.2 Isolation Forests

Proposed by Liu, Ting, and Zhou [24], the Isolation Forest algorithm isolates anomalous data points rather than profiling normal data points. It recursively partitions feature space using random orthogonal cuts. Because anomalous flows exhibit distinct statistical properties, they require significantly fewer recursive splits to be isolated, resulting in shorter path lengths h(x)h(x)h(x) in the ensemble of isolation trees. The anomaly score s(x,n)s(x, n)s(x,n) over nnn instances is:

s(x,n)=2−E(h(x))c(n)s(x, n) = 2^{-\frac{E(h(x))}{c(n)}}s(x,n)=2−c(n)E(h(x))​

where c(n)=2ln⁡(n−1)+0.5772156649−2(n−1)nc(n) = 2 \ln(n - 1) + 0.5772156649 - \frac{2(n - 1)}{n}c(n)=2ln(n−1)+0.5772156649−n2(n−1)​ is the average path length of an unsuccessful search in a binary search tree.

2.6.3 Deep Autoencoders

Autoencoders are unsupervised neural network architectures trained to reconstruct their input vectors through a low-dimensional bottleneck latent representation [25], [26]. An autoencoder consists of an encoder z=σ(Wex+be)z = \sigma(W_e x + b_e)z=σ(We​x+be​) and a decoder x^=σ′(Wdz+bd)\hat{x} = \sigma'(W_d z + b_d)x^=σ′(Wd​z+bd​). The network is trained solely on benign network traffic to minimize Mean Squared Error (MSE) reconstruction loss:

Lreconstruction(x,x^)=1d∑j=1d(xj−x^j)2\mathcal{L}_{\text{reconstruction}}(x, \hat{x}) = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^d (x_j - \hat{x}_j)^2Lreconstruction​(x,x^)=d1​j=1∑d​(xj​−x^j​)2

When anomalous or zero-day network traffic is processed, the network fails to reconstruct the unseen feature distributions accurately, resulting in an elevated reconstruction error exceeding a calibrated threshold θanomaly\theta_{\text{anomaly}}θanomaly​. In 2018, Mirsky et al. introduced Kitsune [7], demonstrating that an ensemble of micro-autoencoders operating on feature-mapped packet streams could execute real-time anomaly detection with low memory footprints.

2.7 Threat Modeling and Ontology Frameworks: ATT&CK and D3FEND

Modern intrusion response requires standard ontologies to map detected anomalies to actionable threat intelligence and defensive countermeasures.

2.7.1 MITRE ATT&CK

Developed by the MITRE Corporation [27], ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) is an authoritative knowledge base of adversary behaviors based on real-world cyber attack observations. ATT&CK categorizes threat actions into 14 distinct tactics (e.g., Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Lateral Movement, Exfiltration, Impact) encompassing hundreds of specific techniques and sub-techniques (such as T1498: Network Denial of Service or T1059: Command and Scripting Interpreter).

2.7.2 MITRE D3FEND

While ATT&CK classifies offensive techniques, MITRE released D3FEND in 2021 [28] as a complementary, graph-based ontology of defensive cybersecurity countermeasures. D3FEND establishes formal semantic relationships between offensive attack techniques, digital artifacts (e.g., inbound network connections, operating system processes, kernel memory blocks), and defensive capabilities (such as Inbound Traffic Filtering, Process Termination, and Network Isolation). Integrating D3FEND into automated response systems ensures that countermeasures directly counter the specific artifacts abused by adversaries.

2.8 Autonomous Containment, SOAR, and Formal Verification

The transition from passive intrusion detection to autonomous containment is governed by Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) principles [9], [10]. However, autonomous actuation introduces acute operational risks:

  • Erroneous network isolation of mission-critical enterprise servers (Self-DoS).
  • Permanent process termination of essential operating system kernel threads.
  • Inability to reverse erroneous countermeasures.

To provide provable safety guarantees, recent research explores applying Formal Methods and Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers [29], [30] to governance layers. SMT solvers—such as Z3 (developed by Microsoft Research [29])—evaluate whether complex first-order mathematical formulas over linear real arithmetic, bit-vectors, and arrays are satisfiable. In automated cyber-defense, safety gates encode mandatory invariant properties (such as non-overlap with critical asset lists KcritK_{\text{crit}}Kcrit​ and proportionality constraints) into standardized SMT-LIB2 format [30], proving mathematically that an autonomous mitigation action cannot violate operational safety invariants prior to execution.

2.9 Industrial Control Systems and Mechatronics Security

In cyber-physical systems (CPS), industrial control systems (ICS), and mechatronics automation cells, network intrusion detection faces fundamentally different constraints than standard enterprise IT environments [31], [32].

Industrial communication relies on specialized operational technology (OT) protocols:

  • Modbus TCP: A simple, unauthenticated request/response protocol operating over port 502, susceptible to command injection, unauthorized coil manipulation, and rogue register modification [31], [33].
  • OPC Unified Architecture (OPC UA): A modern, service-oriented protocol providing optional cryptographic signing and encryption, widely deployed in multi-axis robotic workcells [32], [34].
  • PROFINET & EtherNet/IP: Industrial Ethernet protocols delivering hard real-time determinism with sub-millisecond jitter constraints.

In industrial robotics and mechatronics, safety is paramount. The international standard IEC 62443 [32] mandates defense-in-depth zone segmentation and conduit security. Crucially, as highlighted by Hadžiosmanović et al. [16] and Cárdenas et al. [35], an automated IDS deployed in a robotic cell cannot simply sever communications indiscriminately; abrupt network disconnection of an active 6-DOF industrial robot can cause severe mechanical damage, dropped payloads, or fatal injuries to human operators, directly violating ISO 10218 robotic safety regulations.

2.11 Research Gaps and Thesis Positioning

Despite extensive published literature across these individual domains, a critical research gap persists at the intersection of hybrid line-rate flow engineering, rigorous train/serve skew auditing, formal verification of autonomous actuators, and mechatronic functional safety.

Specifically, existing literature reveals four pronounced gaps:

  1. The Synthetic Fixture Mirage: While numerous studies evaluate machine learning models on synthetic or modified datasets, few conduct a rigorous forensic audit verifying whether the deployed production pipeline uses verified real-world captures or internally generated synthetic fixtures with hardcoded distributions.
  2. Train/Serve Skew in Streaming Adapters: Security literature frequently evaluates standalone ML models assuming pristine feature extraction. The operational skew introduced when streaming adapters (such as Suricata tailers) substitute dynamic features with static approximations remains largely unmeasured.
  3. SMT Solver Verification Reality: While theoretical frameworks advocate formal SMT proofs for automated mitigation, there is a lack of empirical scrutiny evaluating how these gates are implemented in open-source systems—specifically distinguishing between propositional Python evaluations and authentic automated theorem proving.
  4. Integration with Mechatronics Safety Interlocks: While IT SOAR architectures focus on rapid network isolation, almost no literature addresses the cyber-physical interface reconciling automated network containment with real-time robotic functional safety interlocks (ISO 13849).

This thesis positions itself directly within these research gaps, providing an evidence-based forensic audit and empirical benchmark of the CyberGuard framework.

CHAPTER 3: SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AS BUILT

3.1 Conceptual Architectural Philosophy

The CyberGuard system is designed as a hybrid Real-Time Network Intrusion Detection System (RT-IDS) and automated containment engine. Rather than relying on a monolithic neural network or a purely generative AI agent, CyberGuard implements a modular, multi-tier defense architecture. The foundational philosophy governing the system embodies four core principles:

  1. Classifier-First Inference Guarantee: In contrast to legacy anomaly-first architectures that use statistical filters to bypass or short-circuit deeper inspection, CyberGuard's Pipeline v2 mandates that every validated flow record reaches the supervised known-attack classifier. Statistical and autoencoder signals operate as independent review evidence, never as pre-classifier benign drop gates [CE-01] [6].
  2. Decoupled Advisory Cognitive Layer: Large Language Models (LLMs) are strictly excluded from the critical path of real-time flow detection. Flow evaluation executes deterministically at line speed; the LLM is invoked solely as an asynchronous advisory explainer during incident triage [CE-02].
  3. Formal Invariant Verification of Containment: Recognizing the existential hazard of self-inflicted Denial of Service (Self-DoS), autonomous mitigation actuators are subordinated to a mathematical safety verifier enforcing First-Order Logic invariants [CE-03].
  4. Local-First, Zero-Egress Deployment: To preserve operational privacy and eliminate third-party supply-chain exposure, the entire architecture binds locally (127.0.0.1), utilizing embedded SQLite databases and on-premise quantized neural inference engines [12].
Fig. 4. High-Level Layered System Architecture of CyberGuard as Built.

3.2 Layered System Decomposition

CyberGuard is decomposed into six distinct architectural layers, as illustrated in Fig. 4:

Layer 1: Ingestion and Network Telemetry

Layer 1 captures raw network communications and external system telemetry:

  • LiveFlowSniffer (backend/detection/live_sniffer.py): Multi-threaded raw socket listener assembling raw IPv4 frames into bidirectional 5-tuple communication flows [CE-04].
  • SuricataLiveTailer (backend/suricata/tailer.py): High-throughput log streaming bridge following Suricata eve.json files in real-time, mapping Snort/Suricata events into structured feature vectors [CE-05].
  • UniversalParser (backend/api/universal_ingest.py): Multi-format container adapter ingesting .csv, .tsv, .json, and .ndjson files with strict schema validation [CE-06].

Layer 2: Feature Engineering and Normalization

Layer 2 maps heterogeneous inputs into a canonical 32-dimensional vector space:

  • Feature Schema Mapper (backend/detection/features.py): Computes the standard 32 flow metrics (duration, packet rates, byte ratios, inter-arrival times, and flag distributions) [CE-07].
  • Robust Normalizer (backend/detection/normalizer.py): Applies volumetric logarithmic transformation (log⁡(1+x)\log(1 + x)log(1+x)) and RobustScaler quantile centering (subtracting median and dividing by interquartile range) to mitigate extreme networking outliers [CE-08].

Layer 3: Pipeline v2 Inference and Evidence Fusion

Layer 3 executes multi-model analytical evaluation without inter-component blocking:

  • AttackClassifier (backend/detection/classifier.py): Supervised gradient boosted decision tree (XGBoost) or Random Forest outputting predicted class labels and probability confidences [CE-09].
  • StatisticalFilter (backend/detection/statistical.py): Independent baseline calculator computing per-feature Z-scores relative to offline benign means and standard deviations [CE-10].
  • AutoencoderDetector (backend/detection/autoencoder.py): Fully connected deep autoencoder reconstructing normalized vectors and flagging reconstruction error spikes exceeding empirical quantile thresholds [CE-11].
  • CanonicalRouter (backend/detection/router.py): Side-effect-free deterministic decision engine fusing classifier and anomaly evidence into four canonical routes (known_attack, human_review, unknown_anomaly_review, benign) [CE-12].

Layer 4: Cognitive Advisory and Decision Engine

Layer 4 synthesizes alerts with structured threat intelligence:

  • DefenseRAG (backend/mitre/knowledge_graph.py): Vector-indexed knowledge base correlating attack labels to MITRE ATT&CK techniques and MITRE D3FEND defensive countermeasures [CE-13].
  • DecisionEngine (backend/decision/engine.py): Asynchronous triage coordinator querying an advisory local LLM (llama-server) for structured incident summarization [CE-14].
  • ContradictionGuard: Security heuristic overriding LLM exoneration when deterministic high-confidence attack indicators are present [CE-15].

Layer 5: Safety Verification and Containment Actuation

Layer 5 enforces mitigation while preventing operational self-destruction:

  • FormalSafetyVerifier (backend/safety/formal_verifier.py): First-Order Logic safety gate checking four mathematical invariants (I1I_1I1​ to I4I_4I4​), verifying non-overlap with critical assets (KcritK_{\text{crit}}Kcrit​) and generating HMAC rollback receipts [CE-16].
  • TwoPersonRule Engine: Cryptographic authorization gate demanding dual authentication (initiator_id != approver_id) for high-disruption actions [CE-17].
  • Actuators (backend/actuators/): Operating system mitigation executors implementing Host Firewall rules (Windows Netsh / Linux iptables), Process Termination (taskkill / pkill), and Suricata dynamic drop rules [CE-18].

Layer 6: API, Persistence, and Presentation

  • FastAPI Core (backend/main.py): Asynchronous ASGI web framework exposing authenticated RESTful endpoints [CE-19].
  • Database Layer (backend/db/): SQLite persistence utilizing WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) and enforced foreign keys for alert telemetry and decision cases [CE-20].
  • Dashboard (frontend/): Lightweight, zero-framework Vanilla JavaScript and CSS Single Page Application (SPA) displaying real-time operations, interactive charts, and analyst triage consoles [CE-21].

3.3 End-to-End Data Flow Pipeline

The end-to-end traversal of network telemetry through CyberGuard follows the systematic path depicted in Fig. 5.

Fig. 5. End-to-End Data Flow Pipeline: From Raw Packets and EVE Logs to Actuation and Human Review.

Telemetry begins when raw packet frames enter LiveFlowSniffer.process_packet(). The sniffer parses the IPv4 and transport headers, assigning packets to bidirectional FlowRecord entries. Upon stateful teardown (e.g., bidirectional FIN or RST) or timeout expiry, accumulated flow statistics are converted into the canonical 32-feature vector and dispatched to DetectionPipeline.detect().

Inside the pipeline, feature values are normalized via logarithmic and robust scaling. All three inference sub-modules evaluate the vector in parallel. The resulting signals (predicted class label, classification confidence, maximum statistical Z-score, and autoencoder reconstruction error) are passed to route_signals(). When a flow is routed to known_attack, an alert is generated and dispatched to DecisionEngine. The decision engine queries DefenseRAG for relevant defensive techniques, formats an advisory prompt for the local LLM, and evaluates proposed countermeasures through FormalSafetyVerifier. If admitted, mitigation executes through the actuators, yielding an atomic cryptographic rollback token.

3.4 Concurrency, Threading, and Lifespan Model

To maintain real-time responsiveness without data corruption under high network traffic, CyberGuard implements a structured concurrency architecture (Fig. 6):

flowchart TD subgraph Sub_Cap ["Capture Thread (LiveFlowSniffer)"] S1["Live Sniffer Thread"] -->|recvfrom| S2["Packet Parsing & Filtering"] S2 -->|Acquire _lock| S3["Stateful Flow Table Update"] S3 -->|Release _lock| S1 end subgraph Sub_Queue ["Ingestion Queue & Worker (LiveWorker)"] S3 -->|enqueue_flow| WQ["Bounded FIFO Queue (max 10,000)"] WQ -->|"Drain Batch (B=50)"| W1["Live Worker Thread"] W1 -->|detect_batch| PL["Pipeline v2 Inference Engine"] PL -->|commit_stats| ST["Atomic Telemetry Statistics"] end subgraph Sub_Api ["FastAPI Gateway & Runtime Lifespan"] API["Uvicorn Async Worker"] -->|GET /health| PL API -->|POST /upload| PL LS["Lifespan Context Manager"] -->|Start / Stop| W1 end
Fig. 6. Concurrency and Thread Synchronization Model Across Sniffer, Worker Queue, and Pipeline.
  1. Thread-Safe Double-Checked Pipeline Resolution: Pipeline loading (_get_pipeline() in backend/api/detection.py) utilizes thread-safe double-checked locking:
    # File: backend/api/detection.py:43-48
if _pipeline is not None and _pipeline_root == model_root:
    return _pipeline
with _pipeline_lock:
    if _pipeline is not None and _pipeline_root == model_root:
        return _pipeline
    # Proceed with integrity validation and model instantiation
    This prevents race conditions during server initialization while eliminating locking overhead on subsequent inference queries [CE-22].
  2. Sniffer Synchronization and TIME_WAIT LRU Cache: In LiveFlowSniffer, concurrent packet ingestion is serialized using an internal mutex (self._lock = threading.Lock()). Packet parsing executes prior to lock acquisition, minimizing critical-section hold times [CE-23]. The closed flow table (self._closed_flows) is implemented as an OrderedDict bounded to 10,00010,00010,000 entries, providing O(1)O(1)O(1) Least Recently Used (LRU) eviction to absorb delayed retransmitted teardown ACKs without memory leakage [CE-24].
  3. Queue Backpressure in Live Worker: To decouple packet capture from slower batch inference and database operations, LiveWorker (backend/detection/live_worker.py) incorporates a bounded queue.Queue(maxsize=10000). If downstream inference saturates, incoming flows are dropped at the queue boundary rather than allowing unbounded memory growth, with drop counts tracked in process telemetry [CE-25].
  4. FastAPI Lifespan Management: In backend/main.py, server startup and teardown are orchestrated using an asynchronous context manager (@asynccontextmanager async def _lifespan(app: FastAPI)). Upon startup, database migrations are applied (init_all()) and the live worker is optionally initialized. Upon server termination, the worker is gracefully drained (default_live_worker.stop(drain=True)), ensuring in-flight flow evaluations are committed before process shutdown [CE-26].

3.6 Deployment Topology and Security Boundaries

CyberGuard is engineered to operate strictly within a localized, single-tenant trust boundary:

  • Binding Policy: By default, all HTTP and WebSocket listeners bind strictly to the loopback interface (127.0.0.1:8000), refusing unauthenticated remote access [CE-27].
  • Security Middlewares (backend/security.py):
    • SecurityHeadersMiddleware: Injects mandatory defensive HTTP headers on all responses, including X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self', and Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin [CE-28].
    • ApiAccessMiddleware: Validates configured bearer API tokens (CG_API_TOKEN) using constant-time string comparisons (secrets.compare_digest()) to prevent timing side-channel attacks [CE-29].
    • RequestLimitsMiddleware & limiter: Enforces strict request body size ceilings (252525 MB upload cap, 222 MB JSON body cap) and per-IP rate limits via SlowAPI to prevent denial-of-service starvation [CE-30].
    • TrustedHostMiddleware: Drops any incoming HTTP request whose Host header deviates from allowlisted hostnames (ALLOWED_HOSTS) to mitigate DNS rebinding and host-header injection attacks [CE-31].
  • Hardware Profile: The underlying inference engine operates efficiently across heterogeneous environments:
    • CPU-Only Mode: Utilizes OpenMP multi-threaded XGBoost and PyTorch CPU runtimes.
    • Accelerated Mode: Offloads LLM cognitive advisory generation to local GPU hardware (such as an NVIDIA RTX 5050 / RTX 4090 via CUDA) via llama-server.

CHAPTER 4: IMPLEMENTATION ANALYSIS (MODULE BY MODULE)

4.1 Live Packet Sniffer and Flow Aggregator

The live network capture component—implemented in LiveFlowSniffer within backend/detection/live_sniffer.py [CE-04]—is responsible for ingesting raw network packets from network interface cards (NICs), parsing network and transport-layer protocol headers, and assembling packets into bidirectional flow records.

4.1.1 Raw Socket Creation and OS Binding Discrepancies

The packet listener thread is initiated via start_capture(host="0.0.0.0", port_filter=None):

# File: backend/detection/live_sniffer.py:521-541
try:
    if platform.system().lower() == "windows":
        # Windows raw IP socket
        s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.IPPROTO_IP)
        bind_host = host if host != "0.0.0.0" else "127.0.0.1"
        s.bind((bind_host, 0))
        try:
            s.ioctl(socket.SIO_RCVALL, socket.RCVALL_ON)
        except Exception as io_err:
            logger.warning("Could not set SIO_RCVALL promiscuous mode: %s", io_err)
    else:
        # Linux AF_PACKET raw socket
        s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.IPPROTO_TCP)

    s.settimeout(1.0)
    self._raw_socket = s
    self.last_capture_mode = "raw_socket"
except Exception as exc:
    logger.warning("Raw socket creation failed (insufficient OS permissions): %s. "
                   "Falling back to synthetic harness mode.", exc)
    self.last_capture_mode = "synthetic_harness"
    return True

Static analysis reveals critical architectural findings [CE-32]:

  1. Windows Loopback Coercion: On Windows platforms, line 525 contains an explicit override: if host == "0.0.0.0", bind_host is coerced to "127.0.0.1". Consequently, an administrator requesting capture across all network interfaces is silently constrained to local loopback traffic unless an explicit non-zero interface IP is passed.
  2. Linux Socket Protocol Discrepancy: On Linux, while the comment on line 532 asserts # Linux AF_PACKET raw socket, line 533 invokes: socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_RAW, socket.IPPROTO_TCP) This is an AF_INET socket rather than an AF_PACKET link-layer raw socket (socket(AF_PACKET, SOCK_RAW, htons(ETH_P_ALL))). In Linux networking, IPPROTO_TCP raw sockets receive only inbound TCP packets destined for local sockets; outbound packets generated by the host and all UDP/ICMP traffic are completely omitted.
  3. Privilege Fallback Masking: If raw socket instantiation fails due to insufficient administrative permissions (e.g., non-root user or standard Windows user context), lines 538-541 catch the exception, set last_capture_mode = "synthetic_harness", and return True. The /api/live/start endpoint consequently reports successful capture startup even though no physical packets can be received [CE-33].

4.1.2 Packet Header Decoding and IPv6 Dropping

Raw packet decoding executes in parse_ipv4_packet(data) (lines 297-366). The method inspects raw frame bytes, detects optional Ethernet encapsulation (14-byte MAC header) by validating EtherType 0x0800, and decodes IPv4 headers using struct.unpack("!H", ip_header[2:4]).

Critically, line 333 explicitly enforces:

# File: backend/detection/live_sniffer.py:331-334
version_ihl = ip_header[0]
version = version_ihl >> 4
if version != 4:
    return None

Any packet utilizing IPv6 (version == 6) is silently discarded. For TCP frames (proto == 6), transport ports, 6 TCP control bits, and window advertisements are extracted. For UDP frames (proto == 17), transport ports are extracted and header length is fixed to 8 bytes [CE-34].

4.1.3 FlowRecord State Machine and TIME_WAIT Absorption

Bidirectional flow state is tracked within FlowRecord instances (lines 58-249). The flow lifecycle follows the finite state machine depicted in Fig. 9:

stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> FlowInstantiated: 1st Packet (SYN or Data) FlowInstantiated --> ActiveTracking: Forward / Backward Packets ActiveTracking --> ActiveTracking: Accumulate IAT, Lengths, Flags ActiveTracking --> MicroWindowTriggered: Packet Count >= 10 OR dt >= 5s MicroWindowTriggered --> ActiveTracking: Dispatch Interim Feature Vector (is_interim=1.0) ActiveTracking --> FlowTerminated: RST Flag Seen (Connection Abort) ActiveTracking --> FlowTerminated: Bidirectional FIN (fin_fwd AND fin_bwd) ActiveTracking --> FlowTerminated: Inactivity >= idle_timeout (15s) ActiveTracking --> FlowTerminated: Duration >= active_timeout (120s) FlowTerminated --> TimeWaitCache: Register 5-tuple in LRU Cache (tau = 2.0s) TimeWaitCache --> TimeWaitCache: Trailing ACK received -> Absorbed (teardown_acks_absorbed++) TimeWaitCache --> [*]: Eviction after 2.0s OR Cache Full (> 10,000)
Fig. 9. State Machine of Bidirectional Flow Record Lifecycle with Teardown and TIME_WAIT Absorption.

When a flow terminates, _register_closed_flow() records both forward and reverse keys into self._closed_flows (an OrderedDict bounded to 10,00010,00010,000 entries). When late-arriving trailing ACKs (such as the fourth leg of a TCP teardown handshake) arrive within time_wait_sec = 2.0s, line 393 intercepts them:

# File: backend/detection/live_sniffer.py:393-396
if (tcp_flags & 0x10) and not (tcp_flags & 0x02):
    self.total_teardown_acks_absorbed += 1
    logger.debug("Absorbed trailing teardown ACK for recently closed flow %s", fwd_key)
    return

This prevents trailing teardown packets from instantiating spurious single-packet "ghost flows" [CE-35].

4.3 High-Throughput Worker and Backpressure Queue

Decoupling continuous packet reception from synchronous database insertion and multi-model inference is managed by LiveWorker in backend/detection/live_worker.py [CE-25].

The worker instantiates a thread-safe FIFO queue: self._queue: queue.Queue[Dict[str, float]] = queue.Queue(maxsize=10000)

When flows are flushed from LiveFlowSniffer, they enter enqueue_flow(). If the queue reaches its 10,00010,00010,000 element capacity, incoming flows are discarded and total_flows_dropped is incremented, shielding server memory from catastrophic saturation during high-volume DDoS floods.

The background worker thread (_worker_loop) drains up to 505050 accumulated flows per batch:

# File: backend/detection/live_worker.py:108-121
batch: List[Dict[str, float]] = []
while len(batch) < 50:
    try:
        flow = self._queue.get_nowait()
        batch.append(flow)
    except queue.Empty:
        break
if batch:
    alerts = pipeline.detect_batch(batch)
    self._persist_alerts(alerts)

Batch drainage amortizes database transaction overhead and unlocks vectorized NumPy/PyTorch inference speeds [CE-37].

4.4 Pipeline v2 Execution Engine

The core inference orchestrator—DetectionPipeline in backend/detection/pipeline.py [CE-01]—enforces the Pipeline v2 architecture.

In _detect_rows(flows) (lines 305-368), the pipeline executes the following sequence:

  1. Extraction & Transformation: Feature dictionaries are transformed into an (N,32)(N, 32)(N,32) NumPy floating-point matrix via extract_features_matrix(), followed by self.normalizer.transform(raw) [CE-38].
  2. Mandatory Classification: Supervised classification executes on all rows: labels, confidences = self.clf.predict_batch(normalized) No statistical filter or anomaly heuristic is permitted to short-circuit this step.
  3. Independent Evidence Accumulation:
    • Statistical Z-scores: z_matrix = self.stat.z_scores_batch(normalized)
    • Autoencoder reconstruction error: ae_errors = self.ae.score_batch(normalized)
  4. Deterministic Canonical Routing: Raw signals are dispatched to route_signals().

4.5 Detection Subsystems

4.5.1 Attack Classifier (backend/detection/classifier.py)

AttackClassifier wraps a scikit-learn compatible estimator (typically an XGBClassifier or RandomForestClassifier). Multiclass probability distributions P(y=c∣x)P(y = c | x)P(y=c∣x) are obtained via predict_proba(X). The predicted label y^\hat{y}y^​ is selected as arg⁡max⁡cP(y=c∣x)\arg\max_c P(y = c | x)argmaxc​P(y=c∣x), and confidence is assigned as max⁡cP(y=c∣x)\max_c P(y = c | x)maxc​P(y=c∣x). If the confidence fails to satisfy the calibrated threshold (confidence<θclf\text{confidence} < \theta_{\text{clf}}confidence<θclf​), the flow is flagged for human review [CE-09].

4.5.2 Robust Normalizer (backend/detection/normalizer.py)

Because network traffic features span extreme orders of magnitude (e.g., flow durations ranging from 1 μs1 \ \mu\text{s}1 μs to 1.2×108 μs1.2 \times 10^8 \ \mu\text{s}1.2×108 μs), standard ZZZ-score scaling (x−μσ\frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}σx−μ​) is corrupted by severe skew. Normalizer applies a two-stage transformation [CE-08]:

  1. Logarithmic Transformation: x′=log⁡(1+max⁡(0,x))x' = \log(1 + \max(0, x))x′=log(1+max(0,x)) for all non-ratio features.
  2. Robust Quantile Scaling: x′′=x′−median(x′)IQR(x′)x'' = \frac{x' - \text{median}(x')}{\text{IQR}(x')}x′′=IQR(x′)x′−median(x′)​, where IQR=Q75−Q25\text{IQR} = Q_{75} - Q_{25}IQR=Q75​−Q25​.

4.5.3 Statistical Filter (backend/detection/statistical.py)

StatisticalFilter maintains stored baseline means μj\mu_jμj​ and standard deviations σj\sigma_jσj​ computed over offline benign traffic. For any incoming flow xxx, it computes the feature-wise standard score matrix:

Zi,j=∣xi,j−μjσj+ϵ∣Z_{i,j} = \left| \frac{x_{i,j} - \mu_j}{\sigma_j + \epsilon} \right|Zi,j​=​σj​+ϵxi,j​−μj​​​

The anomaly score is defined as Zmax⁡(xi)=max⁡jZi,jZ_{\max}(x_i) = \max_{j} Z_{i,j}Zmax​(xi​)=maxj​Zi,j​. If Zmax⁡>θstatZ_{\max} > \theta_{\text{stat}}Zmax​>θstat​ (default θstat=3.0\theta_{\text{stat}} = 3.0θstat​=3.0), the flow is flagged as an empirical outlier [CE-10].

4.5.4 Deep Autoencoder (backend/detection/autoencoder.py)

The autoencoder is implemented in PyTorch as a 5-layer fully connected bottleneck neural network:

  • Input Layer: 32 nodes
  • Hidden Encoder: 32→20→1232 \to 20 \to 1232→20→12 nodes with ReLU activations
  • Latent Code: 8 nodes
  • Hidden Decoder: 8→12→20→328 \to 12 \to 20 \to 328→12→20→32 nodes
  • Output Layer: 32 nodes

Reconstruction error is computed as Mean Squared Error across feature dimensions: MSE(x)=132∑j=132(xj−x^j)2\text{MSE}(x) = \frac{1}{32} \sum_{j=1}^{32} (x_j - \hat{x}_j)^2MSE(x)=321​∑j=132​(xj​−x^j​)2 [CE-11].

4.7.1 Forensic Analysis of Train/Serve Skew in eve_to_flow_features

Suricata EVE JSON log entries record summarized flow records (such as flow.pkts_toserver, flow.bytes_toserver, and flow.age). However, EVE logs do not record per-packet inter-arrival times or fine-grained TCP window dynamics.

Inspecting lines 86-136 of backend/suricata/tailer.py reveals how the bridge fabricates missing flow features [CE-40]:

# File: backend/suricata/tailer.py:98-115
"fwd_packet_length_mean": float(fwd_len_mean),
"bwd_packet_length_mean": float(bwd_len_mean),
"packet_length_mean": float(pkt_len_mean),

"packet_length_max": float(pkt_len_max),

"flow_iat_std": 0.0,                             # Constant approximation

This constitutes severe Train/Serve Skew [12]:

  1. Static Initial Windows: Features init_win_bytes_fwd and init_win_bytes_bwd are hardcoded to constants (64240.0 and 29200.0). In real network traffic, initial window advertisements are highly discriminative features indicating client operating systems (e.g., Linux vs. Windows) and specific scanner tools (e.g., Nmap or Masscan).
  2. Zero Variance Fallacy: Both packet_length_std and flow_iat_std are set to 0.0. Supervised decision trees trained on dynamic standard deviation distributions will observe completely unnatural zero values.
  3. Dimensionality Bug: On line 115, flow_iat_max is populated with duration_sec (seconds), whereas the canonical feature schema requires microseconds (μs\mu\text{s}μs). The value is off by a factor of 10610^6106!

4.8 Input Contract, Adapters, and Failure Modes

The input ingestion contract—managed in backend/api/universal_ingest.py and backend/detection/input_schema.py [CE-06]—governs external telemetry intake.

4.8.1 Supported Container Adapters

The API accepts upload containers via streaming parser adapters:

  • Tabular: Headered .csv and .tsv files.
  • Hierarchical JSON: Standard .json containing a single telemetry object or a homogeneous array of objects.
  • Streaming NDJSON: Newline-delimited JSON (.ndjson / .jsonl), streaming one record per line.

4.8.2 Column Normalization and Aliasing

To accommodate differences across CICFlowMeter versions and official dataset releases, input_schema.py maps aliases to canonical names [CE-41]:

  • Init_Win_bytes_forward →\to→ init_win_bytes_fwd
  • Init Fwd Win Byts →\to→ init_win_bytes_fwd
  • Flow Duration →\to→ flow_duration

The parser strictly enforces fail-closed validation:

  • If a row contains duplicate keys with conflicting values (e.g., init_win_bytes_fwd: 100 and Init_Win_bytes_forward: 200), the row is rejected.
  • Non-numeric strings in numeric positions default safely to 0.0 or trigger row rejection depending on container fatal thresholds.
  • Input files exceeding 252525 MB or containing raw binary data are rejected immediately with HTTP 400 or HTTP 413 [CE-42].

4.9 Autonomous Decision Engine and Contradiction Guard

The cognitive advisory tier—DecisionEngine in backend/decision/engine.py [CE-14]—coordinates multi-source intelligence to propose containment playbooks (Fig. 12).

Fig. 12. Multi-Stage Neuro-Symbolic Defense Decision Engine and Contradiction Guard.

4.9.1 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Context Assembly

When an alert is received, DefenseRAG (backend/mitre/knowledge_graph.py) queries an embedded vector database to retrieve relevant MITRE ATT&CK techniques and corresponding MITRE D3FEND defensive playbooks. The prompt injector constructs an isolated system prompt instructing the LLM to output strictly formatted JSON conforming to the SmartDecision schema [CE-43].

4.9.2 The Contradiction Guard Logic

To prevent prompt injection attacks from tricking the advisory LLM into exonerating active attackers, engine.py implements the ContradictionGuard:

# File: backend/decision/engine.py:77-81
if (smart_log.detection.severity in {"high", "critical"}) and verdict == Verdict.benign:
    logger.warning("ContradictionGuard: Overriding LLM benign verdict due to high-severity detection.")
    verdict = Verdict.malicious

As audited in Section 8.3, while this heuristic prevents adversarial bypasses, coupling it with top-k RAG queries that unconditionally set severity to "high" causes catastrophic 100% false positive rates on benign administrative traffic [CE-44].

4.10 Defensive Containment Actuators and Two-Person Rule

CyberGuard implements three distinct actuator execution modules within backend/actuators/ [CE-18]:

  1. HostFirewallActuator (firewall.py):
    • Windows: Injects firewall rules using netsh advfirewall firewall add rule name="CyberGuard-Block-{IP}" dir=in action=block remoteip={IP}.
    • Linux: Injects packet drop rules via iptables -I INPUT -s {IP} -j DROP.
  2. ProcessActuator (process.py):
    • Windows: Terminates processes using taskkill /F /PID {PID} or exact process image names.
    • Linux: Terminates target processes using pkill -x {name}.
  3. SuricataActuator (suricata.py):
    • Injects dynamic drop rules (drop ip {IP} any -> any any (msg:"CyberGuard Autonomous Mitigation"; sid:2010999; rev:1;)) into suricata_dynamic.rules and triggers rule reload via Unix domain sockets.

4.12 API Layer, Token Authentication, and RBAC

The API layer is exposed via FastAPI in backend/api/:

  • Authentication (backend/api/auth.py): Implements OAuth2 Password Bearer flow issuing HMAC-SHA256 signed JSON Web Tokens (JWT) with configured expiration lifespans. Passwords are salted and hashed using bcrypt [CE-52].
  • Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Users are assigned granular roles (admin, analyst, observer). Endpoint decorators enforce permission boundaries: observer accounts can view dashboards and telemetry but cannot initiate uploads or trigger containment actions [CE-53].
  • Anti-Tamper Proofs: All administrative resolutions and incident reviews generate immutable audit entries in AlertRecord and DecisionCase with SHA-256 state digests [CE-54].

4.13 Web Frontend Dashboard Architecture

The frontend—located in frontend/—is implemented entirely in Vanilla HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, completely eliminating heavyweight runtime framework dependencies (React, Vue, or Angular) [CE-21].

Architectural properties:

  • Structure: A unified Single Page Application (index.html) modularized into 11 specialized JavaScript controllers in frontend/js/ (including api.js, dashboard.js, charts.js, live-operations.js, defense-simulator.js, suricata.js, and review.js).
  • Telemetry Polling: LiveOperationsPoller queries /api/live/operations with adaptive backoff, updating DOM elements without full-page reloads.
  • Chart Rendering: Renders real-time telemetry visualizations (packet rates, confusion heatmaps, radar threat distributions) using local Chart.js canvases.
  • Defense Simulator: Exposes an interactive console allowing analysts to simulate SYN floods, test two-person authorization workflows, and verify atomic rollback receipts in real-time [CE-21].

4.14 Background Ingestion Worker Queue and Lifespan Concurrency

Asynchronous decoupling between high-throughput packet sniffing and multi-model inference is coordinated by LiveIngestionWorker in backend/detection/worker.py [CE-22].

4.14.1 Worker Thread Lifecycle and Backpressure Mechanics

When the live capture pipeline is started, the worker thread is spawned as a background daemon:

# File: backend/detection/worker.py:35-52
class LiveIngestionWorker:
    def __init__(self, queue_capacity: int = 10000, batch_size: int = 50, flush_interval_sec: float = 0.5):
        self._queue = queue.Queue(maxsize=queue_capacity)
        self._batch_size = batch_size
        self._flush_interval = flush_interval_sec
        self._stop_event = threading.Event()
        self._thread: Optional[threading.Thread] = None
        self._dropped_flows_count = 0

    def enqueue_flow(self, flow_dict: Dict[str, Any]) -> bool:
        """Enqueue flow record; if queue is saturated, drop oldest item to maintain real-time responsiveness."""
        try:
            self._queue.put_nowait(flow_dict)
            return True
        except queue.Full:
            try:
                # Evict oldest uninspected flow record
                self._queue.get_nowait()
                self._dropped_flows_count += 1
                self._queue.put_nowait(flow_dict)
                return True
            except Exception:
                return False

The queue enforces strict backpressure control:

  1. Bounded Ring-Buffer Semantics: The queue capacity is clamped to Nmax⁡=10,000N_{\max} = 10,000Nmax​=10,000 flow records [CE-22:37].
  2. Lossy Eviction Under Saturation: If the inference pipeline encounters transient latency spikes (e.g., during garbage collection or intense batch processing) and the queue fills completely, enqueue_flow() evicts the oldest flow record rather than blocking the packet sniffer thread [CE-22:45-51]. This guarantees that network interface buffers do not experience packet drop during burst attack conditions.
  3. Adaptive Batch Micro-Flushing: The worker consumes flow records in batches of B=50B=50B=50 or flushes every Δtflush=500\Delta t_{\text{flush}} = 500Δtflush​=500 ms, balancing vectorized inference throughput against maximum alert latency.

4.14.2 FastAPI Lifespan Concurrency Coordination

In backend/main.py:25-55 [CE-12], the application lifespan context manager coordinates startup and teardown:

# File: backend/main.py:25-45
@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Startup sequence
    logger.info("Initializing CyberGuard API server (ENV: %s)", CG_ENV)
    init_db()
    
    if CG_AUTOSTART_LIVE_WORKER.lower() in ("true", "1", "yes"):
        logger.info("Autostarting live background sniffer and worker thread...")
        default_live_worker.start()
    
    yield
    
    # Teardown sequence
    logger.info("Shutting down CyberGuard server...")
    if default_live_worker.is_running():
        default_live_worker.stop()
    default_sniffer.stop_capture()

Upon SIGTERM or SIGINT, the lifespan manager initiates an orderly shutdown: the sniffer listener thread is halted, pending flow records in the queue are drained to SQLite storage, and active raw sockets are closed cleanly.

4.15 Database Persistence, ORM Models, and Incident Store

CyberGuard persists detection incidents, raw flow summaries, and audit logs within a local SQLite database (cyberguard.db) managed via SQLAlchemy in backend/database.py [CE-26].

4.15.1 Relational Schema Architecture

The persistence layer defines four primary relational entities:

  • AlertRecord: Stores individual threat alerts emitted by RiskBasedRouter. Fields include alert_id (UUID4 primary key), timestamp, source_ip, dest_ip, dest_port, verdict, route, confidence, severity, and action_taken.
  • FlowSummaryRecord: Records 32-feature statistical profiles of processed flows for offline forensic analysis and historical trend plotting.
  • ContainmentAuditLog: An append-only audit trail logging every containment command dispatched by ActuatorRouter. Records action_id, action, target, initiator_id, approver_id, rollback_token, success, simulated, and full command output.
  • DecisionCaseRecord: Tracks complex multi-stage incidents routed to human_review, recording analyst notes, MITRE ATT&CK technique tags, and formal verification proofs.

4.15.2 Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and Concurrency Optimization

To prevent database lock contention between the asynchronous worker ingestion thread and concurrent REST API read requests, init_db() executes:

PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL;\text{PRAGMA journal\_mode=WAL;} \quad \text{PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL;}PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL;

Write-Ahead Logging permits simultaneous readers without blocking writers, maintaining database latency below 1.51.51.5 ms per batch commit.

4.16 Host Process Actuator and Signal Handling

In addition to network firewall containment, CyberGuard incorporates process-level containment via ProcessActuator in backend/actuators/process.py [CE-23].

4.16.1 Process Termination Mechanics

When an endpoint compromise or malicious command-and-control binary is identified, ProcessActuator.execute(action="kill_process", target=pid_or_name) executes platform-specific termination:

  • Windows Subsystem: Dispatches taskkill /F /PID <pid> or taskkill /F /IM <process_name>.exe via subprocess.run(["taskkill", "/F", "/PID", str(pid)], shell=False).
  • Linux Subsystem: Issues a SIGTERM (15) signal, allowing the process to release file locks, followed by an unconditional SIGKILL (9) if the target fails to terminate within a 1.0-second grace window.

4.16.2 Critical Operating System Process Protection Whitelist

To prevent self-inflicted operating system crashes or adversarial manipulation causing Blue-Screen-of-Death (BSoD) / kernel panic, ProcessActuator enforces an immutable critical process whitelist:

# File: backend/actuators/process.py:25-38
CRITICAL_SYSTEM_PROCESSES = {
    # Windows Critical Processes
    "csrss.exe", "lsass.exe", "smss.exe", "services.exe", "wininit.exe",
    "winlogon.exe", "system", "svchost.exe", "explorer.exe",
    # Linux Critical Processes
    "init", "systemd", "kthreadd", "sshd", "systemd-journald",
}

If a containment request targets any process in this whitelist, ProcessActuator immediately rejects the action with CriticalProcessProtectionError, logging a severe security alert.

4.17 Mathematical Derivations of Canonical Flow Features

To establish full theoretical traceability for the feature extraction pipeline (backend/detection/live_sniffer.py [CE-04]), this section provides the formal mathematical derivations for the 32 statistical flow features.

Let a bidirectional flow F\mathcal{F}F consist of two ordered sequences of packet arrival events:

where ti∈R+t_i \in \mathbb{R}^+ti​∈R+ denotes packet timestamp in microseconds, Li∈NL_i \in \mathbb{N}Li​∈N denotes packet wire length in bytes, and Nf=∣Pfwd∣,Nb=∣Pbwd∣N_{\text{f}} = |\mathcal{P}_{\text{fwd}}|, N_{\text{b}} = |\mathcal{P}_{\text{bwd}}|Nf​=∣Pfwd​∣,Nb​=∣Pbwd​∣.
