8.2 The Synthetic Data Dilemma and Tautological Validation

A critical vulnerability in contemporary machine learning security research is tautological validation [6], [12]: evaluating a model on synthetic test data generated by the exact same parametric distributions used to generate its training set.

8.2.1 The Illusion of High Precision and Recall

On the bundled 2,000-flow evaluation fixture, the XGBoost classifier achieved an overall accuracy of 96.25% and a macro-averaged F1F_1F1​-score of 0.9222 (Table XI). For DDoS and PortScan attacks, both precision and recall reached 100.00%.

However, this performance is a mathematical artifact of the synthetic generator (cyberguard/datasets/generate_sample.py [CE-02]):

  • PortScan flows are synthesized with packet counts strictly between 1≤Npkt≤31 \le N_{\text{pkt}} \le 31≤Npkt​≤3, flow duration <0.05< 0.05<0.05 s, and SYN flags set.
  • DDoS flows are synthesized with packet rates exceeding 1,0001,0001,000 pkts/s and zero backward packets.
  • Benign flows are synthesized with packet rates centered around N(50,152)\mathcal{N}(50, 15^2)N(50,152) pkts/s.

Because these synthetic distributions do not overlap in the feature subspace, the decision tree boundaries converge trivially on synthetic thresholds (e.g., packets_per_sec > 1000 for DDoS).

8.2.2 The Base-Rate Fallacy in Real Deployments

In enterprise production networks, benign network events outnumber true intrusions by orders of magnitude (often 100,000:1100,000:1100,000:1 or 1,000,000:11,000,000:11,000,000:1). Under Axelsson’s base-rate fallacy [13], the Bayesian probability that an alert represents a true intrusion given a positive classification is:

P(Intrusion∣Alert)=P(Alert∣Intrusion)⋅P(Intrusion)P(Alert∣Intrusion)⋅P(Intrusion)+P(Alert∣Benign)⋅P(Benign)(8.1)P(\text{Intrusion} \mid \text{Alert}) = \frac{P(\text{Alert} \mid \text{Intrusion}) \cdot P(\text{Intrusion})}{P(\text{Alert} \mid \text{Intrusion}) \cdot P(\text{Intrusion}) + P(\text{Alert} \mid \text{Benign}) \cdot P(\text{Benign})} \tag{8.1}P(Intrusion∣Alert)=P(Alert∣Intrusion)⋅P(Intrusion)+P(Alert∣Benign)⋅P(Benign)P(Alert∣Intrusion)⋅P(Intrusion)​(8.1)

For CyberGuard’s Bot detection class, our empirical evaluation demonstrated a false positive rate on benign traffic of:

FPRBot=681,600=0.0425(4.25%)\text{FPR}_{\text{Bot}} = \frac{68}{1,600} = 0.0425 \quad (4.25\%)FPRBot​=1,60068​=0.0425(4.25%)

Assuming a realistic intrusion base rate P(Intrusion)=10−4P(\text{Intrusion}) = 10^{-4}P(Intrusion)=10−4 and detection recall P(Alert∣Intrusion)=0.93P(\text{Alert} \mid \text{Intrusion}) = 0.93P(Alert∣Intrusion)=0.93:

P(Intrusion∣Alert)=0.93⋅0.0001(0.93⋅0.0001)+(0.0425⋅0.9999)=0.0000930.000093+0.042496≈0.00218(0.22%)(8.2)P(\text{Intrusion} \mid \text{Alert}) = \frac{0.93 \cdot 0.0001}{(0.93 \cdot 0.0001) + (0.0425 \cdot 0.9999)} = \frac{0.000093}{0.000093 + 0.042496} \approx 0.00218 \quad (0.22\%) \tag{8.2}P(Intrusion∣Alert)=(0.93⋅0.0001)+(0.0425⋅0.9999)0.93⋅0.0001​=0.000093+0.0424960.000093​≈0.00218(0.22%)(8.2)

In a production environment, over 99.78% of Bot alerts would be false alarms. Deploying automated containment under these conditions would inevitably result in widespread self-inflicted denial-of-service across legitimate host processes.

8.3 Architectural Autopsy: The 40/40 False Positive Disaster

The repository's internal stress-test report (MASSIVE_SCALE_ATTACK_STRESS_TEST_REPORT_AR.md [CE-19]) documents a severe operational failure: out of 40 benign administrative activities (such as executing Get-Process | Where CPU -gt 10, running nightly mysqldump backups, running CI/CD test runners, or scraping Prometheus metrics), 40 out of 40 were classified as malicious attacks (100% false alarm rate).

Our forensic investigation traced this failure to a catastrophic coupling across three independent components:

Fig. 24. Root-cause fault tree illustrating the three-stage architectural coupling that produced the 40/40 (100%) false positive disaster.

8.3.1 Forensic Trace of the Coupling

  1. Unconditional Top-KKK Retrieval Bias: When telemetry is ingested, default_defense_rag.retrieve_playbook(query, k=4) executes a vector similarity search across MITRE ATT&CK embeddings. The retriever lacks a similarity threshold cutoff (τsim=0.65\tau_{\text{sim}} = 0.65τsim​=0.65). Even if cosine similarity is near zero, the engine unconditionally returns four techniques (e.g., T1190: Exploit Public-Facing Application and T1071: Standard Application Layer Protocol).
  2. Heuristic Severity Over-Coupling: In backend/ingestion/universal_parser.py:72, the parser contains the following line:
    severity = "high" if len(matched_techniques) >= 2 or iocs["cve_identifiers"] else "medium"
    Because the RAG engine unconditionally returns four techniques (k=4≥2k=4 \ge 2k=4≥2), every single ingested log event is tagged as severity: "high", regardless of content.
  3. Contradiction Guard Over-Suppression: In the decision engine (backend/decision/engine.py:79), a safety rule was implemented to prevent adversarial prompt injection from duping the advisory LLM into acquitting genuine attacks:
    if (smart_log.detection.severity in {"high", "critical"}) and verdict == Verdict.benign:
    verdict = Verdict.malicious
    Because Defect 2 tagged all traffic as severity: "high", whenever the advisory LLM correctly recognized a benign administrative script and emitted Verdict.benign, the Contradiction Guard forcibly overruled the LLM, flipped the verdict to Verdict.malicious, and dispatched automated host containment!

8.3.2 The Advisory LLM Latency Bottleneck

In addition to the false positive crisis, the stress test recorded decision latencies of:

  • Median (P50P_{50}P50​): 27.5527.5527.55 seconds
  • 90th Percentile (P90P_{90}P90​): 34.5134.5134.51 seconds
  • 99th Percentile (P99P_{99}P99​): 42.3442.3442.34 seconds

With inference latencies approaching 30 to 45 seconds per incident, an attacker executing automated port scanning or credential stuffing (generating 500 requests per second) easily outpaces the decision engine by four orders of magnitude, causing unbounded queuing memory growth and complete defense paralysis.

8.3.3 Quality Gate Evolution Discrepancy: Conflicting-Label Deduplication

During our static AST audit of candidate promotion workflows in backend/detection/candidate_workflow.py, we identified an architectural divergence in the implementation of the no_exact_or_near_conflicting_label_duplicates quality gate:

  1. Original Upload Version (CyberGuard-feature-ai-active-defense): In backend/detection/candidate_workflow.py:766-768 (in the original upload branch commit), the quality gate was defined as:

    "no_exact_or_near_conflicting_label_duplicates": not any(
    duplicate_conflicts.values()
),

    In this earlier version, the gate strictly required zero conflicting-label duplicate groups across exact and log-rounded near feature hashes (not any(duplicate_conflicts.values())). If identical or near-identical feature rows carried conflicting class labels, the candidate training pipeline failed its validation gates (failed_gates).

  2. Current Branch Version (feature/realtime-ids-pipeline): In backend/detection/candidate_workflow.py:766-768, the gate logic is defined as:

    "no_exact_or_near_conflicting_label_duplicates": (
    set(map(int, train["row_hashes"])).isdisjoint(set(map(int, final["row_hashes"])))
),

    In this branch, the gate name is retained unchanged, but the underlying predicate evaluates only that the row-hash sets of the training partition and the final evaluation partition are disjoint. Meanwhile, lines 634–650 continue to compute the duplicate_conflicts metrics (exact_conflicting_label_rows, near_conflicting_label_rows, exact_conflicting_label_feature_groups, near_conflicting_label_feature_groups) and serialize them into split_manifest.json (line 663), but duplicate_conflicts no longer gates candidate promotion. Additionally, static grep inspection confirms that no automated unit or integration test in tests/ references or asserts this quality gate.

8.5 Threats to Validity

8.5.1 Internal Validity

  1. Synthetic Traffic Bias: The bundled model relies entirely on synthetic flow fixtures. While synthetic data guarantees complete test reproducibility, it lacks genuine TCP congestion dynamics and multi-protocol multiplexing.
  2. Measurement Latency Overhead: Python latency measurements were performed using time.perf_counter_ns(). While monotonic and high-resolution, Python GIL thread preemption and OS scheduling jitter introduce minor noise into single-flow tail latency measurements (P99P_{99}P99​).
  3. Conflicting Duplicate Resolution Variance: The candidate pipeline silently favors whichever class appears first in CSV order when resolving identical feature vectors with conflicting ground-truth labels (Decision D1), introducing order-dependent stochastic variance into internal validation.

8.5.2 External Validity

  1. Single Third-Party Dataset Mirror: The candidate pipeline is evaluated exclusively on CICIDS2017 retrieved from a third-party Hugging Face mirror (bencorn/CICIDS2017). Cryptographic integrity against the original UNB generation remains unverified. No cross-dataset evaluation on modern benchmarks (such as CSE-CIC-IDS2018 or TON_IoT) was conducted.
  2. Extreme Class Imbalance and Tiny Classes: The evaluation partition contains microscopic representation for critical threats (Infiltration N=7N=7N=7, WebAttack N=107N=107N=107, Bot N=113N=113N=113), rendering reported per-class metrics statistically volatile or uninterpretable.
  3. No Live End-to-End Network Evaluation: Due to the absence of raw PCAPs, mathematical equivalence between CICFlowMeter's offline Java feature generation and CyberGuard's live CPython packet sniffer could not be verified on identical packets.

8.5.3 Construct Validity

  1. Feature Set Expressiveness: CyberGuard’s 32 flow features measure duration, packet sizes, and flag counts. They do not inspect encrypted TLS SNI, JA3/JA4 cryptographic fingerprints, or deep application layer protocol commands. Modern adversaries utilizing HTTPS/WebSocket C2 channels with normal packet sizing can completely evade statistical flow boundaries.

8.6 Hostile Examiner Defense: 20 Core Challenges and Definitive Responses

To ensure maximum academic rigor and anticipate critical skepticism from doctoral examination tribunals and senior security auditors, this section articulates the twenty most demanding technical challenges that can be leveled against CyberGuard, followed by uncompromising, evidence-grounded responses.

Challenge 1: The Synthetic Accuracy Tautology

Examiner Question: "You report a 96.25% accuracy and 0.9222 macro-F1 score for your supervised classifier. However, our audit reveals that the model was trained and evaluated on synthetic data generated by cyberguard/datasets/generate_sample.py using a hardcoded seed (seed=42). Isn't this reported performance scientifically meaningless and purely tautological?"
Author Response: Yes, absolutely. As formally stated in Section 8.2 and documented in our Claims Ledger (CLM-004, CLM-007), the reported 96.25% accuracy is a mathematical artifact of fitting gradient-boosted decision trees to non-overlapping synthetic Gaussian and uniform distributions. When evaluated against real CICIDS2017 traffic (Section 6.8.3), accuracy collapses from 96.25% down to 38.15%, Macro-F1F_1F1​ falls to 0.0757, and the model falsely flags 55.07% of all benign flows as attacks (189,977 false alarms).

Challenge 2: The Autoencoder Anomaly Saturation Collapse

Examiner Question: "Your experimental results show that the deep autoencoder flagged 100.0% of benign flows as anomalies, with mean reconstruction errors (8.1×1098.1 \times 10^98.1×109) exceeding the stored threshold (0.0045970.0045970.004597) by nine orders of magnitude. Why did this catastrophic calibration failure occur, and why was it not caught during development?"
Author Response: The failure is rooted in a critical pre-processing pipeline mismatch: CyberGuardPipelineV2 (backend/detection/pipeline.py:170-185 [CE-05]) standardizes features using normalizer.pkl before passing them to the XGBoost classifier, but forwards the unnormalized, raw feature vector directly to autoencoder.forward(). Because features such as Flow Duration (≈107 μs\approx 10^7\ \mu\text{s}≈107 μs) and Flow Bytes/s (≈106 B/s\approx 10^6\ \text{B/s}≈106 B/s) have values orders of magnitude larger than the normalized unit-variance inputs on which the autoencoder's linear projection layers were trained, the network experiences severe numerical saturation, driving the Mean Squared Error to billions.

Challenge 3: Inbound-Only Linux Raw Socket Blinding

Examiner Question: "Line 533 of backend/detection/live_sniffer.py instantiates socket(AF_INET, SOCK_RAW, IPPROTO_TCP) on Linux, while line 532 asserts # Linux AF_PACKET raw socket. In Linux network architecture, doesn't an IPPROTO_TCP raw socket receive only inbound TCP segments destined for the local host, completely blinding the IDS to outbound exfiltration, link-layer frames, UDP floods, and ICMP scans?"
Author Response: Confirmed. This is an indisputable architectural defect in the ingestion engine (CLM-009). An AF_INET raw socket with IPPROTO_TCP only receives incoming TCP packets that match local host IP addresses. It does not receive outbound traffic generated by compromised local processes, transit traffic forwarded across a gateway router, connectionless UDP traffic, or ICMP network sweep probes. To function as a true network-wide intrusion detector, the socket must be rewritten to bind link-layer raw frames via socket(AF_PACKET, SOCK_RAW, htons(ETH_P_ALL)) or utilize AF_XDP / eBPF kernel bypass [19].

Challenge 4: Windows Loopback Interface Coercion

Examiner Question: "In backend/detection/live_sniffer.py:525, if an administrator specifies host = "0.0.0.0" on a Windows host, the code forcibly overrides this to bind_host = "127.0.0.1". How can an enterprise intrusion detection system operate if binding to all network interfaces silently restricts packet capture to local loopback traffic?"
Author Response: Confirmed. On the Windows operating system, raw socket capture across all interfaces via SIO_RCVALL promiscuous mode requires binding to the explicit IPv4 address assigned to the target physical Network Interface Card (NIC). Because binding to INADDR_ANY (0.0.0.0) fails on the WinSock2 provider, the developer introduced line 525 as an ad-hoc fallback. Consequently, unless an operator manually discovers and passes their physical Ethernet/Wi-Fi IP via configuration, CyberGuard silently inspects only local loopback IPC communications.

Challenge 5: Suricata Bridge Train/Serve Skew

Examiner Question: "In backend/suricata/tailer.py:98-115, your EVE-JSON parser fabricates initial TCP window values as static constants (64,240 and 29,200 bytes), sets packet length standard deviation to zero, and passes flow duration in seconds into a feature field expecting microseconds. Doesn't this invalidate any machine learning inference performed on Suricata telemetry?"
Author Response: Yes. This is a severe instance of train/serve feature skew [12]. As empirically proven in our skew ablation experiment (Table XI-H), evaluating the candidate model with Suricata-approximated features causes Macro-F1F_1F1​ to collapse to 0.2840, and drives the Attack Miss Rate to 98.59%, rendering the model completely blind to live attacks.

Challenge 6: FastAPI Application Metadata Contradiction

Examiner Question: "In backend/main.py:59-65, the FastAPI application description explicitly states: 'Live packet ingestion and automated response are not implemented.' This directly contradicts your thesis title and documentation. Is the system an illusion?"
Author Response: This represents a case of documentation-code divergence during iterative refactoring. The modules backend/detection/live_sniffer.py and backend/actuators/router.py were implemented in full, but the static string in main.py was left un-updated from an earlier scaffolding prototype. Furthermore, CG_AUTOSTART_LIVE_WORKER defaults to "false" in config.py:75 (CLM-019), meaning that upon launching uvicorn backend.main:app, the live ingestion worker does not automatically start unless the operator explicitly issues a POST request to /api/live/start or sets CG_AUTOSTART_LIVE_WORKER=true.

Challenge 7: Propositional Boolean Logic vs. Authentic SMT Verification

Examiner Question: "You market your safety containment gate as utilizing 'Formal First-Order Logic SMT Verification', citing SMT-LIB2 standards. Yet, lines 185–204 of formal_verifier.py reveal that it merely invokes SymPy's propositional satisfiable() over four Python booleans (inv_c, inv_o, inv_b, inv_p), while lines 246–270 format an inert string template. Isn't calling this an SMT solver fundamentally inaccurate?"
Author Response: The criticism is fully valid. As documented in Chapter 4 and Table XVIII, no authentic SMT solver process (such as Z3 [29] or CVC5) is ever spawned or executed by FormalSafetyVerifier. The implementation evaluates simple propositional conjunctions (admitted=I1∧I2∧I3∧I4\text{admitted} = I_1 \land I_2 \land I_3 \land I_4admitted=I1​∧I2​∧I3​∧I4​) over four pre-evaluated booleans. Formatting the result into an SMT-LIB2 text template string serves solely as an exportable audit certificate, not a formal mechanical proof.

Challenge 8: The 40/40 False Alarm Disaster on Benign Operations

Examiner Question: "The repository's internal stress-test report (MASSIVE_SCALE_ATTACK_STRESS_TEST_REPORT_AR.md) documents that 40 out of 40 benign administrative operations (PowerShell Get-Process, database backups mysqldump, Nessus scans, Prometheus scraping) were flagged as attacks. How can an autonomous defense system be considered remotely usable when its false positive rate on administrative traffic is exactly 100%?"
Author Response: The system in its audited state is completely unusable for production deployment without remediation. As proven in our architectural autopsy (Section 8.3), this disaster was caused by the unfortunate coupling of three design flaws:

  1. default_defense_rag unconditionally retrieves the top 4 ATT&CK techniques with zero cosine similarity cutoff (τsim\tau_{\text{sim}}τsim​).
  2. universal_parser.py:72 sets severity = "high" whenever ≥2\ge 2≥2 techniques are returned, making 100% of logs 'high' severity.
  3. decision/engine.py:79 forcibly converts any benign LLM verdict to Verdict.malicious if severity is 'high'.

Challenge 9: The 27-Second LLM Advisory Decision Bottleneck

Examiner Question: "Your stress-test report documents median decision latencies of 27.55 seconds (and 99th percentile latencies of 42.34 seconds) on the advisory LLM path. How can CyberGuard claim to provide 'real-time active defense' when modern automated exploits breach systems in milliseconds?"
Author Response: The 27.55-second latency is an inherent bottleneck of running multi-turn local 8B parameter models (Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct) on consumer GPU hardware (NVIDIA RTX 5050) under multi-threaded concurrency. We concur that 27 seconds is orders of magnitude too slow for real-time line-rate mitigation. Our architectural analysis demonstrates that the cognitive LLM reasoning engine must be decoupled from the inline packet path: line-rate fast-path mitigation must execute via deterministic, low-latency rules (<5< 5<5 ms), while the LLM operates strictly out-of-band as an asynchronous Tier-3 strategic advisor (Section 10.2).

Challenge 10: Model Serialization and Deserialization Security

Examiner Question: "CyberGuard loads trained model artifacts via Python pickle and joblib. Since pickle is known to execute arbitrary code via __reduce__ gadgets, what prevents an attacker who gains access to the filesystem from achieving full root/administrator remote code execution?"
Author Response: CyberGuard mitigates casual tampering through its pre-deserialization manifest check validate_artifact_bundle() (backend/detection/integrity.py:402-439 [CE-11]), which computes streaming SHA-256 digests and validates non-symlink constraints prior to deserialization. However, as we critically proved in Section 7.2.3, the manifest artifacts.json itself is unsigned. If an attacker possesses local write privileges to data/models/trained/, they can overwrite both classifier.pkl and update artifacts.json with the new SHA-256 hash. To achieve true production-grade defense, the manifest must be signed using an asymmetric Ed25519 digital signature verified against a hardcoded public key.

Challenge 11: Unauthenticated Loopback Privilege Elevation

Examiner Question: "In backend/auth.py:313-318, unauthenticated requests arriving from loopback (127.0.0.1) are automatically assigned Role.ADMIN if CG_ENV != "production". Doesn't this allow any local unprivileged process or browser-based SSRF exploit to execute arbitrary administrative containment actions?"
Author Response: Yes, this is a severe authorization vulnerability (CLM-046). The loopback bypass was implemented as a convenience for local developer workflows, but in a production or shared workstation environment, it completely invalidates the RBAC perimeter. Any co-located web service vulnerable to Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), or any malicious website visited by an administrator that issues cross-origin fetch requests to http://localhost:8000/api/actuators/execute, can trigger destructive network containment without supplying credentials. We recommend immediate deprecation of loopback auto-elevation (Table XX).

Challenge 12: Silent Dropping of IPv6 Network Frames

Examiner Question: "Line 333 of live_sniffer.py enforces if version != 4: return None, silently dropping all IPv6 frames. In modern enterprise environments where IPv6 represents 30% to 50% of internal traffic, isn't this an unacceptable blind spot?"
Author Response: Yes. Any adversary operating over IPv6 (e.g., SLAAC spoofing, IPv6 tunneling, or direct IPv6 port scanning) can execute attacks completely invisible to CyberGuard's live sniffer. The packet decoding pipeline must be updated with an RFC 8200 compliant 40-byte IPv6 header parser capable of traversing extension header chains (Hop-by-Hop, Routing, Fragment).

Challenge 13: Non-Functional Active and Idle Mean Features

Examiner Question: "Features #31 (Active Mean) and #32 (Idle Mean) are declared in your canonical 32-feature dictionary, yet lines 234–235 of live_sniffer.py permanently hardcode both values to 0.0. Why are these features retained if they are never computed?"
Author Response: These features were retained to preserve dimensional compatibility with the pre-trained XGBoost model weights, which expect exactly 32 input dimensions matching the legacy CICFlowMeter schema [1]. Because tracking true active/idle transmission bursts requires maintaining timer state across micro-pauses within open connections, the sniffer implementation omitted the calculation and defaulted both fields to zero. This introduces permanent feature distortion for protocols characterized by bursty transmission.

Challenge 14: Insider Threat and Two-Person Rule Tampering

Examiner Question: "Your Two-Person Rule implementation in backend/actuators/router.py:73-110 checks that initiator_id and approver_id are both provided and distinct. However, if the API caller simply passes two arbitrary strings (initiator_id="alice", approver_id="bob"), what prevents a single rogue operator from fabricating an approver identity?"
Author Response: In the current implementation, if the API caller possesses valid API tokens or operates under the loopback bypass, the router verifies only that the string fields are populated and non-identical; it does not currently cross-reference the approver against an active cryptographic session or require a distinct secondary digital signature. In Section 7.4.1 and Table XX, we recommend hardening the Two-Person Rule to require dual-signed JWT challenge-response authentication, where the approver must independently sign the containment proposal using their own private key.

Challenge 15: Cyber-Physical Containment Risks in Mechatronics

Examiner Question: "Your thesis proposes extending CyberGuard to industrial mechatronic workcells (Chapter 9). However, if an IDS autonomously drops network communication to a multi-axis articulated robot or CNC spindle, won't this trigger uncontrolled mechanical crashes, tool breakage, or operator injury?"
Author Response: We address this exact hazard in Chapter 9 (Section 9.4). In an industrial mechatronic cell, standard network containment (e.g., iptables DROP) is strictly prohibited. Cutting fieldbus traffic while a robot arm moves at high speed risks severe collisions or gravitational dropping of unbraked axes. Our proposed architecture integrates directly with certified Safety PLCs, commanding an IEC 60204-1 Category 1 Controlled Safe Stop (controlled trajectory deceleration before removing motor power). Autonomous IT defense must never override physical functional safety interlocks.

Challenge 16: Third-Party Mirror Provenance and Unverified Upstream Checksums

Examiner Question: "Your manifest declares that the candidate model was trained on CICIDS2017 downloaded from a third-party Hugging Face mirror (bencorn/CICIDS2017). The manifest states checksum_provenance: observed_unb_archive_checksum. Does this represent a cryptographic proof that the dataset matches the original 2017 University of New Brunswick archive?"
Author Response: No. As documented in Section 5.2.2, the string observed_unb_archive_checksum merely denotes the SHA-256 hashes observed from the extracted archive on the Hugging Face repository. Because the official University of New Brunswick (UNB) web portal does not publish signed, direct single-file HTTPS SHA-256 manifests for these specific extracted CSV tables without human form interactions, cryptographic integrity between this third-party mirror and the original 2017 UNB generation is formally unverified. We state plainly that the experimental data originates from a third-party mirror.

Challenge 17: Silent Duplicate Conflict Resolution and First-Seen Bias (Decision D1)

Examiner Question: "In backend/detection/trainer.py:221-254, the code discovers 6,132 exact and 3,228 near duplicate groups where identical flow features map to conflicting ground-truth labels (e.g., Benign vs. DDoS). Rather than rejecting ambiguous data or raising an IntegrityError, the code silently resolves conflicts by keeping the first row observed in CSV order. Doesn't this inject arbitrary file-order bias into model learning?"
Author Response: Yes, this is an undeniable methodological defect (Decision D1). As experimentally proven in our duplicate policy sensitivity analysis (Table XI-G, Policy 3), randomly shuffling CSV ingestion order alters which ground-truth label wins in conflicting groups, causing model Macro-F1F_1F1​ to fluctuate across seeds. When conflicting rows are completely purged (Policy 2), Macro-F1F_1F1​ improves from 0.7763 to 0.7899, and Bot F1F_1F1​ increases from 0.5917 to 0.6624. Silently resolving contradictions by CSV order polutes the training boundary with mislabeled flows.

Challenge 18: Within-Session Capture-Group Split Optimism (Decision D2)

Examiner Question: "The candidate training pipeline partitions each (capture, class) into 5 sequential row blocks, holding out the 5th block (20%) as test data. Isn't this an optimistic within-session holdout that leaks temporal correlation across interleaved flows, rather than evaluating true temporal generalization?"
Author Response: Yes. The split method name capture_group is misleading: it does not hold out distinct capture sessions, but rather takes a 20% slice from every capture file. In our day-disjoint experiment (Table XI-F, Section 6.8.4), where models were trained on Monday–Wednesday captures and evaluated on Thursday–Friday captures, the model suffered a 65.69% silent miss rate on unseen attack families and detected 0 out of 1,489 Thursday BruteForce attacks. The within-session split severely masks real-world temporal vulnerability.

Challenge 19: Unsupervised Autoencoder Multi-Day Drift (Decision D3)

Examiner Question: "Your autoencoder is trained strictly on the first 100,000 benign rows (Decision D3). On the real test partition, benign flows exhibit a mean reconstruction error of 11,488.1, whereas attack flows exhibit a mean error of 4,126.7. Why is the reconstruction error inverted, with clean traffic generating higher errors than attacks?"
Author Response: This inverted error anomaly is a direct consequence of truncating training to the first 100,000 benign rows (Monday morning baseline). As network usage shifts throughout the week, benign office traffic introduces novel web protocols, larger MTU sizes, and bursty transfers that were never observed in the first 100,000 rows. Meanwhile, volumetric attack floods (such as DoS Hulk) are characterized by repetitive, low-variance packet streams that compress into lower latent reconstruction errors. Unsupervised anomaly detection on this feature set completely breaks down under natural temporal drift.

Challenge 20: Train/Serve Feature Skew and Operational Inability to Detect Attacks Live (Decision D4)

Examiner Question: "Your candidate model achieves a 0.6852 Macro-F1 on static CSV tables. But in live serving, your sniffer hardcodes active_mean and idle_mean to 0.0, and cannot extract initial TCP window sizes from Suricata logs. What is the candidate model's actual performance when deployed behind CyberGuard's live ingestion engine?"
Author Response: The candidate model severely degrades under live serving features (Decision D4). As measured in our feature skew ablation experiment (Table XI-H), forcing features to the sniffer's runtime defaults causes Macro-F1F_1F1​ to drop from 0.6852 down to 0.3668, while the Attack Miss Rate increases from 7.16% to 40.79%. However, it is essential to qualify that this 0.3668 figure represents a pessimistic worst-case lower bound, simulating flows intercepted mid-stream without observing the initial TCP SYN handshake (or across UDP/ICMP traffic); during standard live operation with observed handshakes, LiveFlowSniffer actually extracts initial TCP window sizes (live_sniffer.py:133), so everyday operational degradation would be less extreme. In contrast, the Suricata bridge scenario represents a definitive static failure mode: because backend/suricata/tailer.py:108-124 permanently hardcodes static window constants (64240.0 and 29200.0) and zero variances across 100% of translated records, 98.59% of all attacks are missed (Macro-F1=0.2840F_1 = 0.2840F1​=0.2840). Furthermore, when retrained from scratch without the four skewed features, the model achieves Macro-F1=0.5983F_1 = 0.5983F1​=0.5983, representing a true degradation of Δ≈−0.1780\Delta \approx -0.1780Δ≈−0.1780 against the clean 32-feature full retrain baseline (0.7763). Because the model was trained on offline features that live components either approximate poorly or hardcode to constants, the candidate model cannot function as an effective real-time detector in its current state.

CHAPTER 9: MECHATRONICS PERSPECTIVE: PROTECTING INDUSTRIAL ROBOTICS AND OT NETWORKS

[!NOTE] Architectural Status Disclaimer: The frameworks, protocol extensions, and containment interlocks detailed in this chapter represent a proposed theoretical adaptation and hardening roadmap engineered specifically for industrial automation and robotic control environments. They are not part of the baseline CyberGuard IT implementation audited in Chapters 4–8. All designs are formally grounded in international cyber-physical security standards (IEC 62443 [32], NIST SP 800-82 [31], ISO 13849-1).

9.1 Cyber-Physical Systems and the Mechatronics Threat Landscape

Modern mechatronic systems—such as 6-DOF articulated industrial robot arms, automated guided vehicles (AGVs), multi-axis CNC milling centers, and distributed manufacturing workcells—are no longer isolated electromechanical islands [31]. The integration of Industry 4.0 paradigms, Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) sensors, and remote diagnostic telemetry has interconnected Operational Technology (OT) fieldbuses with enterprise IT networks and cloud telemetry brokers [32], [39].

9.1.1 The Inverted Security Triad

In enterprise IT networks, the classical security triad prioritizes Confidentiality, followed by Integrity, with Availability third (C→I→AC \to I \to AC→I→A). In mechatronic and industrial control systems (ICS), this hierarchy is strictly inverted [31], [35]:

Mechatronics Priority:Safety & Availability≫Integrity≫Confidentiality(9.1)\text{Mechatronics Priority:} \quad \mathbf{\text{Safety \& Availability}} \gg \mathbf{\text{Integrity}} \gg \mathbf{\text{Confidentiality}} \tag{9.1}Mechatronics Priority:Safety & Availability≫Integrity≫Confidentiality(9.1)

Table XIX contrasts enterprise IT networks against mechatronic OT networks across key operational dimensions.

TABLE XIX. COMPARATIVE MATRIX: ENTERPRISE IT NETWORKS VS. MECHATRONIC OT FIELD NETWORKS
Parameter / Dimension Enterprise IT Environment (CyberGuard Baseline) Mechatronic & Industrial OT Workcell (Proposed Adaptation)

Acceptable Cycle Jitter Hundreds of milliseconds (100−500100-500100−500 ms tolerated) Strict microsecond-to-millisecond determinism (Δt≤1−10\Delta t \le 1-10Δt≤1−10 ms)

9.1.2 Adversarial Attack Vectors Against Industrial Robots

An adversary penetrating the field network of an industrial robotics cell targets the physical dynamics of the machinery [40], [41]:

  1. Kinematic Boundary Override: Modifying trajectory setpoints in PLC memory registers (e.g., target joint positions θi\theta_iθi​ or angular velocities θ˙i\dot{\theta}_iθ˙i​) to force a robotic manipulator outside its authorized safety enclosure into human-occupied workstations.
  2. Dynamic Jerk and Resonance Attacks: Injecting high-frequency alternating command oscillations designed to excite the natural mechanical resonant frequencies (ωn\omega_nωn​) of gearboxes and harmonic drives, inducing premature structural fatigue and mechanical failure without triggering simple threshold alarms [35].
  3. Sensor Spoofing and Feedback Manipulation: Intercepting optical encoder feedback or force/torque sensor telemetry via Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) ARP spoofing, misleading closed-loop PID controllers into applying excessive motor torque.
  4. Denial-of-Control (DoC) Flooding: Flooding the real-time Ethernet interface (e.g., PROFINET or Modbus TCP port 502) with malformed frames, causing the real-time communications coprocessor to miss heartbeat deadlines and triggering uncoordinated emergency halts (E-Stops) that damage delicate in-process workpieces [31], [40].

9.2 Limitations of Standard IT-NIDS in Industrial Workcells

Deploying an IT-oriented intrusion detection system like baseline CyberGuard directly onto an industrial mechatronics bus introduces severe operational risks:

  1. Uncalibrated Feature Extraction: CyberGuard’s 32 flow features measure duration, byte ratios, and TCP flags designed for web and DNS traffic. In an industrial cell running Modbus TCP or PROFINET, packet lengths are static (e.g., exactly 64 bytes for cyclical polling) and inter-arrival times are rigidly fixed to the PLC scan cycle (e.g., Δtscan=10.0\Delta t_{\text{scan}} = 10.0Δtscan​=10.0 ms). As proven in Chapter 6, baseline CyberGuard's autoencoder and statistical detector flag 100% of non-standard flows as anomalous, which would cause permanent alert saturation in an OT environment.
  2. Blindness to Semantic Payload Attacks: An attacker modifying a Modbus register from 0x0000 (safe speed) to 0xFFFF (maximum dangerous speed) generates a packet that is syntactically flawless from a TCP/IP perspective. A flow-based detector inspecting only header flags and durations is completely blind to this catastrophic payload alteration [16].
  3. Catastrophic Unilateral Containment: In baseline CyberGuard, the ActuatorRouter issues host-level commands (New-NetFirewallRule or iptables DROP). In an industrial workcell, abruptly severing network communication to a multi-axis servo drive while in motion can cause gravitational collapse of heavy vertical axes or uncoordinated collisions with transfer presses. Containment must strictly interface with functional safety systems [31], [32].

9.3 Proposed Real-Time Mechatronic IDS (RT-M-IDS) Architecture [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

To bridge the gap between IT intrusion detection and cyber-physical safety, we propose an architectural extension: the Real-Time Mechatronic Intrusion Detection System (RT-M-IDS). (Note: The RT-M-IDS and all its constituent sub-modules described in this section represent a proposed conceptual roadmap and are NOT IMPLEMENTED in the CyberGuard codebase.)

Fig. 25. Proposed Real-Time Mechatronic IDS (RT-M-IDS) architecture incorporating passive optical network taps, deep OT protocol parsing, kinematic state-space anomaly detection, and functional safety PLC containment interlocks [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED].

9.3.1 Passive Network Ingestion [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

To guarantee zero latency impact on industrial control loops, the proposed RT-M-IDS design connects exclusively via passive optical TAPs or hardware-isolated SPAN mirror ports on the managed field switch. Under this proposed design, the appliance would operate in pure promiscuous listen-only mode, with physical transmit (TX) fibers detached to make packet injection back into the control loop physically impossible at the physical layer.

9.3.2 Deep OT Protocol Ingestion Layer [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

The proposed ingestion engine conceives protocol-specific decoders for industrial fieldbuses (not present in the repository code):

  • Modbus TCP Decoder [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]: Proposed to decode the 7-byte Modbus Application Protocol (MBAP) header: Transaction ID, Protocol ID (0x0000), Length, Unit ID, and extract Function Codes (0x01 Read Coils, 0x03 Read Holding Registers, 0x05 Write Single Coil, 0x10 Write Multiple Registers) alongside target 16-bit register addresses and values [31], [33]. (Note: The repository's backend/suricata/ module parses only IT Suricata EVE-JSON events; no OT or Modbus binary decoders exist in the repository code).
  • OPC UA Decoder [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]: Proposed to inspect OPC UA binary conversation streams (opc.tcp://), verifying Secure Channel IDs, Authentication Tokens, and monitoring WriteRequest services targeting robot control nodes [34]. (Note: No OPC UA decoders exist in the repository code).

9.3.3 Physics-Grounded State-Space Anomaly Detection [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

9.4 Functional Safety Containment Interlocks (IEC 60204-1 / ISO 13849) [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

In a mechatronic environment, autonomous containment cannot utilize operating system firewall rules. Under this proposed design, containment must strictly interface with functional safety architectures conforming to IEC 60204-1 (Safety of machinery - Electrical equipment of machines) and ISO 13849-1 (Performance Level e, Category 4) [31], [32].

9.4.1 Safe Stop Categories Under Attack Mitigation [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

The proposed containment engine specifies one of three standardized stop protocols per IEC 60204-1:

  1. Stop Category 2 (Controlled Stop with Drive Power Maintained): Used for low-severity policy violations (e.g., unauthorized diagnostic query from a maintenance laptop). The robot is brought to a controlled deceleration stop along its programmed path. Motor torque is maintained to hold position without tripping the physical safety circuit.
  2. Stop Category 1 (Controlled Deceleration with Power Cut): Used for cyber-physical attacks commanding out-of-boundary setpoints. Power is maintained to the servo drives while an active deceleration trajectory is executed to bring the arm to a controlled rest in ≈250\approx 250≈250 ms. Once stationary, mechanical holding brakes engage and drive power is de-energized via Safe Torque Off (STO). This prevents the mechanical damage associated with violent emergency clamping.
  3. Stop Category 0 (Immediate Uncontrolled Power Removal): Reserved strictly for imminent physical collision or human enclosure boundary breach. Drive electrical power is immediately severed, and spring-actuated mechanical holding brakes clamp instantly.

9.4.2 Hardware Safety PLC Interlock [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

To implement this mitigation safely, the proposed RT-M-IDS edge appliance does not communicate directly with the servo inverters over Ethernet. Instead, the appliance would trigger a hardwired, fail-safe dual-channel relay output (dry contact) connected directly to the Safety PLC's digital input modules (e.g., Siemens S7-1500F or Beckhoff TwinSAFE).

The Safety PLC evaluates the hardware signal within its certified safety task cycle (1−21-21−2 ms), executing certified safety function blocks (SF_EmergencyStop or SF_SafeStop1) independently of the non-safe software runtime. This guarantees that a software crash within the AI detection appliance can never prevent or subvert the safety shutdown of the physical machine.

9.5 Case Study: 6-DOF Robotic Welding Workcell [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

To theoretically ground the proposed mechatronic framework, we examine an architectural case study: an automated automotive spot-welding workcell powered by a 6-DOF articulated robot arm controlled by a PLC communicating over Modbus TCP. (Note: This case study is an architectural simulation scenario; neither the physical workcell nor the robotic interlock software is present in the repository).

9.5.1 Attack Scenario

An external adversary compromises an engineering workstation on the enterprise network and pivots across the IT/OT boundary firewall into the manufacturing VLAN. The adversary initiates a Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) ARP spoofing attack between the Human-Machine Interface (HMI) and the cell PLC:

  • Malicious Payload: The adversary transmits Modbus TCP Function Code 0x10 (Write Multiple Registers), targeting holding registers 40100-40105 (Joint 2 and Joint 3 target positions).
  • Adversarial Objective: Command Joint 2 to rotate from 45∘45^\circ45∘ to 165∘165^\circ165∘ at maximum torque (100%100\%100% velocity setpoint), deliberately causing the welding gun to strike a fixture clamping jig at high speed, inflicting severe mechanical destruction and halting the automotive assembly line.

9.5.2 Detection and Containment Execution

  1. Passive Ingestion (0 ms inline overhead): The passive optical tap mirrors the raw Modbus frame to the RT-M-IDS edge appliance.
  2. Protocol Parsing (14.2 μs\mu\text{s}μs): The Modbus parser decodes MBAP transaction 0x8FA2, Unit ID 0x01, Function Code 0x10, Register 40100, Length 6.
  3. Whitelist & Physics Validation (48.6 μs\mu\text{s}μs):
    • Rule Check: The origin IP (192.168.10.155, maintenance laptop) is not in the authorized HMI whitelist for write operations (violates IEC 62443 zone policy).
    • Kinematic Check: Forward kinematic projection calculates that the commanded Joint 2 position (165∘165^\circ165∘) places the end-effector outside the safe bounding geofence Vsafe\mathcal{V}_{\text{safe}}Vsafe​, projecting an impact in Δt=380\Delta t = 380Δt=380 ms.
  4. Safety Interlock Dispatch (1.2 ms):
    • The RT-M-IDS safety gate asserts its hardware dry-contact output to the Safety PLC.
    • The Safety PLC initiates an immediate Category 1 Safe Stop: servo inverters execute controlled dynamic braking along the current trajectory, halting all motion in 185185185 ms, 195195195 ms prior to predicted mechanical impact.
  5. Perimeter Network Isolation: The appliance issues a signed rollback receipt to the industrial perimeter switch via 802.1X quarantine, isolating the compromised maintenance laptop port from the factory floor.
  6. Post-Incident Forensic Receipt: An immutable incident receipt is generated, recording the exact Modbus frame payload, the violated kinematic invariant equations, and the Safety PLC deceleration telemetry, enabling rapid root-cause analysis by certified automation engineers.

9.6 Mathematical Kinematics and Dynamic Singularity Analysis [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

To detect sophisticated cyber-physical attacks that evade simple static threshold rules, the proposed RT-M-IDS formulation embeds a rigorous analytical kinematics model of the monitored manipulator [35], [41]. (Note: This mathematical model is a proposed analytical formulation not implemented in repository code).

Kinematic Singularity Threat: A kinematic singularity occurs when the Jacobian matrix loses full rank:

det⁡(J(θ))=0(9.11)\det(\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta})) = 0 \tag{9.11}det(J(θ))=0(9.11)

In the vicinity of a singularity (e.g., wrist alignment θ5=0\theta_5 = 0θ5​=0 or boundary extension θ3=0\theta_3 = 0θ3​=0), computing the inverse kinematics requires:

θ˙=J−1(θ)vTCP(9.12)\dot{\boldsymbol{\theta}} = \mathbf{J}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) \mathbf{v}_{\text{TCP}} \tag{9.12}θ˙=J−1(θ)vTCP​(9.12)

As det⁡(J)→0\det(\mathbf{J}) \to 0det(J)→0, elements of J−1\mathbf{J}^{-1}J−1 approach infinity (∥J−1∥→∞\|\mathbf{J}^{-1}\| \to \infty∥J−1∥→∞). A stealthy adversary who injects modest Cartesian velocity commands vTCP\mathbf{v}_{\text{TCP}}vTCP​ directing the robot into a singular configuration induces extreme, uncommanded angular accelerations (θ¨i→∞\ddot{\theta}_i \to \inftyθ¨i​→∞) at the joint actuators, tripping over-current protection, stripping harmonic gear teeth, or violently flinging the workpiece [41].

Under the proposed analytical formulation, the RT-M-IDS evaluates the manipulability measure w(θ)w(\boldsymbol{\theta})w(θ):

w(θ)=det⁡(J(θ)JT(θ))(9.13)w(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \sqrt{\det(\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\mathbf{J}^T(\boldsymbol{\theta}))} \tag{9.13}w(θ)=det(J(θ)JT(θ))​(9.13)

If a network command produces a state trajectory where w(θ)<ϵsingularityw(\boldsymbol{\theta}) < \epsilon_{\text{singularity}}w(θ)<ϵsingularity​ while commanded Cartesian velocity remains non-zero, the packet would be intercepted as an adversarial singularity attack.

9.7 OT Protocol Frame Forensics and Byte-Level Dissection [PROPOSED DESIGN - NOT IMPLEMENTED]

To illustrate the concrete protocol parsing required by the proposed RT-M-IDS, this section provides an authentic byte-level dissection of synthetic Modbus TCP traffic constructed for our theoretical workcell evaluation:

9.7.1 Modbus TCP Protocol Data Unit (PDU) Architecture

Modbus TCP encapsulates the classical Modbus Remote Terminal Unit (RTU) application protocol within TCP port 502, substituting the CRC16 trailer with a 7-byte Modbus Application Protocol (MBAP) header:

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           MBAP Header (7 Bytes)                         |
+-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+-------------+
| Transaction ID    | Protocol ID       | Length            | Unit ID     |
| (2 Bytes)         | (2 Bytes, 0x0000) | (2 Bytes)         | (1 Byte)    |
+-------------------+-------------------+-------------------+-------------+
|                           Modbus PDU (Variable)                         |
+-------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+
| Function Code     | Data Payload (Register Addresses, Counts, Values)   |
| (1 Byte)          | (Variable)                                          |
+-------------------+-----------------------------------------------------+

CHAPTER 10: RECOMMENDATIONS, FUTURE WORK, AND CONCLUSION

10.1 Synthesis of Critical Findings

This thesis has presented an exhaustive, empirical, and architectural evaluation of the CyberGuard Real-Time Intrusion Detection and Autonomous Containment System. By executing rigorous code forensics, static AST dependency mapping, and reproducible empirical benchmarks across five dedicated test harnesses, we evaluated the system against both its published specifications and foundational network security principles.

10.1.1 Architectural Strengths

Our audit identified notable architectural strengths within the codebase:

  1. High Ingestion Efficiency: The standalone user-space packet parser in LiveFlowSniffer achieves a sustained in-memory parsing throughput of 718,569 packets per second (1.392 μs\mu\text{s}μs per packet) in single-threaded user space on synthetic frames. While this provides sufficient headroom for medium and standard MTU-sized Gigabit traffic (Table VIII-B), it represents an in-memory parsing upper bound (excluding kernel syscalls, queue contention, feature extraction, and ML inference) and falls short of line rate for minimum 64-byte frames (1.488 Mpps).
  2. Deterministic Flow Lifecycle Management: The FlowRecord finite state machine correctly manages bidirectional connection tracking, absorbing trailing teardown ACKs without spawning phantom sessions and supporting early micro-window feature extraction for rapid attack classification (Table VII).
  3. Defense-in-Depth Model Integrity: CyberGuard acknowledges the inherent risks of Python pickle deserialization, enforcing pre-deserialization SHA-256 checksum validation, non-symlink verification, and schema hash binding in validate_artifact_bundle() prior to loading serialized model weights (Fig. 22).
  4. Formal Containment Safety Interlocks: The formal safety verification gate (FormalSafetyVerifier) successfully intercepts destructive containment actions, preventing self-denial-of-service against loopback addresses, default gateways, public DNS resolvers, critical operating system processes, and neutralizing shell injection attempts (Table XIV).
  5. Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards: For live containment enforcement, the ActuatorRouter strictly enforces the Two-Person Rule, requiring distinct initiator and approver identities and generating cryptographically signed HMAC-SHA256 rollback receipts for atomic state reversion (Fig. 23).

10.1.2 Critical Architectural Vulnerabilities and Model Findings

Our empirical evaluations across both model pipelines uncovered critical vulnerabilities that preclude production deployment:

  1. The Synthetic Training Fixture Trap (Bundled Model): The shipped XGBoost classifier was trained exclusively on a synthetic, parametric sample dataset (artifacts.json: production_approved=false, seed 42) spanning only four basic classes. When evaluated against real network traffic, the model collapses down to 38.15% accuracy and 0.0757 Macro-F1F_1F1​, while falsely flagging 55.07% of all benign flows as attacks (189,977 false alarms out of 344,984 clean flows), proving that synthetic fixtures provide zero real-world operational protection.
  2. The Candidate Real-Data Model Reality (candidate_cicids2017): While trained on 2,096,796 real flows from CICIDS2017, the candidate pipeline remains strictly unpromoted (shadow_only_not_promoted, production_approved=false). Although its headline accuracy (0.9849) and Weighted-F1F_1F1​ (0.9855) appear high, they are heavily masked by the 84.8% prevalence of Benign traffic. Unweighted Macro-F1F_1F1​ reaches only 0.6852 [95% CI: 0.6447, 0.7133], unmasking fatal operational blind spots: complete detection collapse on Botnet C2 traffic (0.00% recall, 0.00 F1F_1F1​; 113/113 flows missed) and severe precision collapse on PortScan (0.1862).
  3. Four Critical Methodological Decisions:
    • Decision D1 (Conflicting Duplicate Policy): backend/detection/trainer.py:221-254 silently resolves 6,132 exact and 3,228 near conflicting duplicate groups by first-seen CSV order, injecting arbitrary order-dependent label bias while relaxing promotion gates (candidate_workflow.py:766-768).
    • Decision D2 (Within-Session Split Optimism): The capture_group split slices each capture session into 5 contiguous row blocks, masking a 65.69% silent miss rate on novel attacks exposed under true day-disjoint temporal evaluation (Mon–Wed train vs. Thu–Fri test).
    • Decision D3 (Autoencoder Truncation Anomaly): Training the PyTorch autoencoder strictly on the first 100,000 benign flows creates multi-day temporal drift, causing benign test traffic to exhibit higher mean reconstruction error (11,48811,48811,488) than attack traffic (4,1264,1264,126), inverting the anomaly detection signal.
    • Decision D4 (Train/Serve Feature Skew): The candidate model expects 32 features, but the live sniffer hardcodes active_mean and idle_mean to 0.0 and cannot extract initial TCP window sizes, collapsing candidate Macro-F1F_1F1​ from 0.6852 down to 0.3668 (40.79% attack miss rate). Under Suricata approximations, the attack miss rate surges to 98.59%.
  4. Autoencoder Calibration Collapse (Bundled Model): Due to an unscaled feature mismatch between data pre-processing and model evaluation, the bundled deep PyTorch autoencoder exhibits an empirical reconstruction error nine orders of magnitude above its calibrated threshold (8.1×1098.1 \times 10^98.1×109 vs. 0.0045970.0045970.004597), flagging 100.0% of all flows as anomalous and corrupting downstream risk-based routing (Table XII).
  5. OS Raw Socket Limitations: On Linux, the sniffer binds an AF_INET socket with IPPROTO_TCP, capturing only inbound TCP traffic and completely blinding the system to link-layer frames, outbound flows, UDP floods, and ICMP probes. On Windows, binding 0.0.0.0 is silently coerced to 127.0.0.1, and IPv6 frames are discarded universally (Chapter 4).
  6. Loopback Administrative Elevation: In non-production environments where CG_ENFORCE_AUTH != "true", any unauthenticated client connecting over loopback is automatically elevated to Role.ADMIN, creating severe exposure to SSRF and browser-based cross-site port attacks (Chapter 7).
  7. The 40/40 False Positive Disaster & Latency Bottleneck: Unconditional top-kkk RAG retrieval coupled with a flawed severity heuristic in universal_parser.py and over-suppression in engine.py caused a 100% false positive rate on benign administrative scripts, while the local LLM advisory path incurred an unworkable median decision latency of P50=27.55P_{50} = 27.55P50​=27.55 seconds (Chapter 8).
  8. Core Scientific Limitations: The real-data evaluation is bounded by five unavoidable constraints: (i) reliance on a third-party Hugging Face mirror with unverified upstream University of New Brunswick checksums; (ii) documented labeling and flow bugs inherent to CICIDS2017 [15]; (iii) microscopic support for critical minority classes (Infiltration N=7N=7N=7); (iv) lack of cross-dataset generalization against a secondary benchmark (such as CSE-CIC-IDS2018); and (v) absence of live end-to-end packet PCAP replay to confirm Java-vs-Python feature equivalence.

10.3 Future Research Directions

Beyond immediate codebase remediation, the findings of this thesis motivate four vital avenues of future research:

10.3.1 Kernel-Bypass Packet Ingestion via eBPF and XDP

While Python raw sockets achieved 718 Kpps in user space, carrier-grade 10 Gbps and 100 Gbps interfaces process between 14.88 and 148.8 million packets per second. Future iterations of CyberGuard should migrate the packet filtering and flow state machine into the Linux kernel using eBPF (Extended Berkeley Packet Filter) and XDP (eXpress Data Path) [19]. By executing flow aggregation directly within the network interface driver before socket allocation, line-rate throughput can be sustained with zero user-kernel context switching overhead.

10.3.2 Non-Stationary Temporal Learning and Conformal Prediction

To overcome the synthetic data trap, future models must be trained on authentic, multi-day benchmark datasets (such as CSE-CIC-IDS2018 or UNSW-NB15) utilizing strict temporal train-test partitioning (the TESSERACT methodology [22]). Furthermore, rather than relying on arbitrary confidence thresholds (e.g., τclf=0.90\tau_{\text{clf}} = 0.90τclf​=0.90), models should incorporate inductive conformal prediction. Conformal prediction provides mathematically guaranteed coverage error bounds, allowing the detector to output prediction sets rather than point predictions and provably controlling false alarm rates under non-stationary distribution drift.

10.3.3 Authentic SMT-Solver Verification Over Dynamic Network Graphs

While the current verifier checks static boolean invariants, true autonomous containment requires reasoning over dynamic, multi-hop network topologies. By embedding an authentic SMT solver such as Z3 [29], the safety subsystem can express first-order relational constraints:

∀u,v∈Vnet,Connected(u,v)∧IsCritical(u)  ⟹  ¬IsolatesPath(action,u,v)(10.1)\forall u, v \in \mathcal{V}_{\text{net}}, \quad \text{Connected}(u, v) \land \text{IsCritical}(u) \implies \neg \text{IsolatesPath}(\text{action}, u, v) \tag{10.1}∀u,v∈Vnet​,Connected(u,v)∧IsCritical(u)⟹¬IsolatesPath(action,u,v)(10.1)

This guarantees that an automated firewall rule isolating an infected host never severs redundant communication paths between critical supervisory controllers and industrial field actuators.

10.3.4 Hardware-in-the-Loop Validation for Industrial Mechatronics

Building upon the theoretical framework established in Chapter 9, future work should deploy and benchmark the proposed RT-M-IDS architecture on physical mechatronic hardware. Deploying the appliance onto an experimental testbed featuring a 6-DOF industrial manipulator (e.g., KUKA KR-6 or ABB IRB-120) communicating over Modbus TCP and OPC UA will enable empirical measurement of physical deceleration profiles, bus jitter, and real-time fault injection resilience under live kinematic attacks.

10.4 Conclusion

Autonomous network defense represents the frontier of modern cybersecurity engineering. As attack automation accelerates, human security operations centers (SOCs) can no longer manually triage, investigate, and contain complex volumetric and multi-stage cyber threats within sub-second reaction windows.

However, as demonstrated throughout this thesis, the transition from human analysis to automated artificial intelligence introduces acute architectural hazards. Uncalibrated anomaly thresholds, synthetic dataset overfitting, and brittle heuristic-LLM couplings can transform an autonomous defense system into an engine of self-inflicted denial-of-service.

The central lesson of the CyberGuard evaluation is that machine learning classification must never act with unconstrained authority. True operational resilience requires an uncompromising synthesis: pairing high-throughput statistical pattern recognition with formal symbolic safety gates, rigorous cryptographic integrity boundaries, and fail-safe physical interlocks. Only when machine intelligence is bounded by deterministic mathematical invariants can autonomous systems be safely entrusted with the defense of our critical digital and cyber-physical infrastructures.

Appendix D: Step-by-Step Reproduction Guide and Production Manifests

To ensure absolute scientific and engineering reproducibility, this appendix provides the complete environment commands, empirical harness execution sequences, and production container orchestration manifests.

D.1 Prerequisites and Environment Setup

  • Operating System: Windows 10/11 (x86_64) or Linux (Ubuntu 22.04 LTS / Debian 12 recommended)
  • Python: Python 3.12 (64-bit)
  • Node.js: Node.js v20+ (with npm 10+)
  • System Memory: Minimum 8 GB RAM (16 GB recommended)

Clone or navigate to the workspace root:

cd .

Create and activate a clean virtual environment:

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Install core dependencies pinned to compatible releases:

pip install --upgrade pip
pip install fastapi==0.110.0 uvicorn==0.28.0 scikit-learn==1.4.1.post1 xgboost==2.0.3 torch==2.2.1 sympy==1.12 pandas==2.2.1 numpy==1.26.4 pytest==8.1.1 pytest-json-report==1.5.0

D.2 Executing Empirical Verification Harnesses

Execute the empirical benchmark suite in order. All scripts deposit structured JSON results directly into report/results/:

  1. Verify Full Pytest Suite (536 tests):
    pytest -q
  2. Execute Sniffer Micro-Benchmarks (718k PPS & state transitions):
    python report/experiments/exp_p3b_sniffer.py
  3. Execute Pipeline Benchmarks (Latency percentiles & batch scaling):
    python report/experiments/exp_p3c_pipeline.py
  4. Execute Model Evaluation (Classifier accuracy & autoencoder divergence):
    python report/experiments/exp_p3d_model_eval.py
  5. Execute Robustness & Adversarial Perturbation Tests:
    python report/experiments/exp_p3e_robustness.py

D.3 Executing Citation Engine TDD Tests

Validate citation numbering order, range compression, and missing key fail-closed behavior:

pytest report/tests/test_citations.py -v

D.4 Compiling the Master's Thesis Technical Report

The build pipeline compiles all Markdown chapters into a unified HTML document with KaTeX equations, Mermaid diagrams, and Paged.js running headers/footers, exporting to print-ready PDF:

node report/build.mjs

The compiled report artifacts will be generated under:

  • report/dist/report.html (Interactive, self-contained single-page report)
  • report/dist/report.pdf (Print-ready, paginated A4 master document)

D.5 Production Multi-Stage Hardened Dockerfile

Listing D.1 presents the production multi-stage Docker build specification enforcing non-root execution and minimal attack surface.

# Listing D.1: Production Multi-Stage Dockerfile (Dockerfile.production)
# Stage 1: Build Environment
FROM python:3.12-slim-bookworm AS builder

WORKDIR /build
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential libpcap-dev && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --user -r requirements.txt

# Stage 2: Minimal Hardened Runtime
FROM python:3.12-slim-bookworm AS runner

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    libpcap0.8 libcap2-bin iptables curl && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Create unprivileged system user
RUN groupadd -g 1001 cyberguard && \
    useradd -u 1001 -g cyberguard -s /usr/sbin/nologin -M cyberguard

WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /home/cyberguard/.local
COPY --chown=cyberguard:cyberguard . /app

ENV PATH=/home/cyberguard/.local/bin:$PATH \
    PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    CG_ENV=production \
    CG_AUTOSTART_LIVE_WORKER=true

# Grant packet sniffing capability without full root
RUN setcap cap_net_raw,cap_net_admin+ep /usr/local/bin/python3.12

USER cyberguard
EXPOSE 8000

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=10s --retries=3 \
    CMD curl -f http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/health || exit 1

ENTRYPOINT ["uvicorn", "backend.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

D.6 Multi-Container Production Orchestration Specification

Listing D.2 provides the production docker-compose.production.yml orchestrating Suricata sensor capture, CyberGuard pipeline processing, Redis task queuing, and Prometheus metrics scraping.

# Listing D.2: Production Docker Compose Orchestration (docker-compose.production.yml)
version: '3.8'

services:
  suricata:
    image: jasonish/suricata:7.0.3
    container_name: cyberguard-suricata
    network_mode: host
    cap_add:
      - NET_ADMIN
      - NET_RAW
      - SYS_NICE
    volumes:
      - ./config/suricata.yaml:/etc/suricata/suricata.yaml:ro
      - suricata-logs:/var/log/suricata
    restart: unless-stopped

  cyberguard-core:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile.production
    container_name: cyberguard-core
    network_mode: host
    environment:
      - CG_ENV=production
      - CG_DATABASE_URL=sqlite:////app/data/cyberguard.db
      - CG_REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6379/0
      - CG_AUTOSTART_LIVE_WORKER=true
      - CG_SURICATA_EVE_PATH=/var/log/suricata/eve.json
    volumes:
      - cyberguard-data:/app/data
      - suricata-logs:/var/log/suricata:ro
    depends_on:
      - redis
    restart: unless-stopped

  redis:
    image: redis:7.2-alpine
    container_name: cyberguard-redis
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:6379:6379"
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    restart: unless-stopped

  prometheus:
    image: prom/prometheus:v2.50.0
    container_name: cyberguard-prometheus
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:9090:9090"
    volumes:
      - ./config/prometheus.yml:/etc/prometheus/prometheus.yml:ro
      - prometheus-data:/prometheus
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  suricata-logs:
  cyberguard-data:
  redis-data:
  prometheus-data:

Appendix E: Formal Neuro-Symbolic Safety Gate Specification and SMT-LIB2 Encodings

This appendix provides the formal mathematical and logical specification of CyberGuard's Neuro-Symbolic Safety Gate (backend/safety/formal_verifier.py [CE-18]), including the complete truth table evaluation across all 16 possible boolean assignments and the standard SMT-LIB2 theory representation.

E.1 Complete 16-Row Propositional Truth Table

The formal safety gate evaluates four boolean variables:

  • b1b_1b1​: allow_high_risk_remediation (Administrative flag permitting destructive intervention)
  • b2b_2b2​: manual_override (Human-in-the-loop manual confirmation)
  • b3b_3b3​: quarantine_requested (Autonomous engine requests network/process quarantine)
  • b4b_4b4​: unverified_anomaly (Detection signal is based solely on uncalibrated anomaly scores)

The fundamental safety invariant IsafeI_{\text{safe}}Isafe​ mandates:

Isafe=¬(b3∧b4∧¬b2)∧(b3∧¬b1  ⟹  b2)(E.1)I_{\text{safe}} = \neg \left( b_3 \land b_4 \land \neg b_2 \right) \land \left( b_3 \land \neg b_1 \implies b_2 \right) \tag{E.1}Isafe​=¬(b3​∧b4​∧¬b2​)∧(b3​∧¬b1​⟹b2​)(E.1)

As proven by the truth table, exactly 3 of the 16 states (Rows 2, 3, and 11) violate the safety specification and are deterministically blocked by the safety gate.

E.2 SymPy Abstract Syntax Tree Reduction

In backend/safety/formal_verifier.py, SymPy constructs a boolean logic Abstract Syntax Tree (AST):

# SymPy Propositional Invariant Reduction
from sympy import symbols, Not, And, Implies
b1, b2, b3, b4 = symbols("b1 b2 b3 b4")
c1 = Not(And(b3, b4, Not(b2)))
c2 = Implies(And(b3, Not(b1)), b2)
formula = And(c1, c2)

Applying boolean distribution and De Morgan's laws:

c1=¬b3∨¬b4∨b2c_1 = \neg b_3 \lor \neg b_4 \lor b_2c1​=¬b3​∨¬b4​∨b2​
c2=¬(b3∧¬b1)∨b2=¬b3∨b1∨b2c_2 = \neg (b_3 \land \neg b_1) \lor b_2 = \neg b_3 \lor b_1 \lor b_2c2​=¬(b3​∧¬b1​)∨b2​=¬b3​∨b1​∨b2​

Conjoining the clauses yields the simplified Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF):

Isafe=(¬b3∨b2∨¬b4)∧(¬b3∨b2∨b1)I_{\text{safe}} = (\neg b_3 \lor b_2 \lor \neg b_4) \land (\neg b_3 \lor b_2 \lor b_1)Isafe​=(¬b3​∨b2​∨¬b4​)∧(¬b3​∨b2​∨b1​)

Factoring out common terms (¬b3∨b2)(\neg b_3 \lor b_2)(¬b3​∨b2​):

Isafe=(¬b3∨b2)∨(¬b4∧b1)(E.2)I_{\text{safe}} = (\neg b_3 \lor b_2) \lor (\neg b_4 \land b_1) \tag{E.2}Isafe​=(¬b3​∨b2​)∨(¬b4​∧b1​)(E.2)

This mathematical reduction proves that the safety check requires only a single 2-term boolean expression, demonstrating that invocation of general symbolic solver engines is redundant for this logic.

E.3 SMT-LIB2 Standard Benchmark Script

Listing E.1 presents the valid SMT-LIB2 benchmark script that can be verified by any standard compliant SMT solver (e.g., Microsoft Z3).

; Listing E.1: CyberGuard Safety Invariants in SMT-LIB2 Format (safety.smt2)
(set-logic QF_BOOL)
(set-info :source |CyberGuard Formal Safety Invariant Benchmark|)
(set-info :status sat)

; Declare boolean propositions
(declare-fun allow_high_risk () Bool)
(declare-fun manual_override () Bool)
(declare-fun quarantine_requested () Bool)
(declare-fun unverified_anomaly () Bool)

; Safety Clause 1: Never quarantine on unverified anomaly without manual override
(assert (not (and quarantine_requested unverified_anomaly (not manual_override))))

; Safety Clause 2: Quarantine without high-risk permission mandates manual override
(assert (=> (and quarantine_requested (not allow_high_risk)) manual_override))

(check-sat)
(get-model)
(exit)

Executing z3 safety.smt2 confirms that the invariant system is satisfiable (sat) and yields consistent counterexample models when an unsafe assertion is introduced, verifying the formal correctness of the underlying propositional design.
